speechtext:
I should like to ask the Minister of Justice a question. I do not want to oppose the bill in any respect, but we spent a whole day last session considering what should be done about the great loss of life in Canada through motor accidents on the highways. A private bill was presented and the minister promised that during the recess of parliament he would look into the matter. We are sitting here as the high court of parliament and all that needs to be done under this section is for provincial magistrates and judges to notify the registrar of motor 
vehicles of a conviction. Surely the government have a better policy than that. The minister promised to look into the great loss of life and the large number of injuries caused by accidents in Canada on highways and at level crossings. What has the government done to lessen this great loss of life, either by legislation under the code or otherwise? For the last five years I have introduced substantive motions and bills introduced in this connection but nothing has been done. In England they have done a great deal towards reducing the number of deaths in automobile accidents. I would not like to see the Minister of Justice injured by some motor car, but even in front of these buildings one has to step pretty lively at times to avoid motor cars. When we see men, women and children slaughtered in Canada as they are, I believe the penalties should be more severe than anything we have adopted as yet. This section provides:
-the court or justice may . . . make an order prohibiting such person from driving a motor vehicle or automobile anywhere in Canada during any period not exceeding three years. In the event of such an order being made the court or justice shall forward a copy thereof to the registrar of motor vehicles for the province wherein a permit or licence to drive a motor vehicle or automobile was issued to such person.
I do not see that this is necessary, because most of these charges are laid, not under the code, but under the different motor vehicles acts. The Ontario act has been amended to cover just this point, and surely if that is all we are going to do we shall continue to have this great loss of life in Canada. There were eighty people killed and nearly 2,500 injured on the streets of Toronto last year. Why, you could fill every seat in this House of Commons with the number of people killed in this way in three large cities of this country. Should we not do something more than merely notify the highway departments of the various provinces? That is provided for now in four or five provinces; when magistrates or justices of the peace register convictions it is their duty under the highway traffic act to take the action that is proposed under this section. Surely with all these commissions roaming around the country a matter concerning the very life of thousands of our people could be better dealt with. I do not want members of the cabinet to be killed on the highways, but even on this speedway in front of the building we all have to watch very carefully, because we never know who is going to be killed next.
I want to ask the minister if he will not consider, during the recess of parliament, a thorough national investigation into this great

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
loss of life to which I have referred, with a view to taking steps such as those that have been taken in England, where they have drastically reduced the number of accidents of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says the motor vehicle act of Ontario, provides for what is contained in this amendment, but the Ontario act applies only to that province. This is to make this provision applicable to the whole of Canada, and it has been requested by persons and governments interested in this matter.
In regard to the stringency of the law concerning motor accidents, that question was thoroughly considered last year, when amendments were made to our code after consultation with attorneys general and others. I believe the law now is as severe as it can be. My hon. friend has been advocating that we should follow the law of England in the matter. We did; we brought in amendments last year which made our law similar to the English law. I am afraid there will always be accidents unless we entirely prohibit the use of motor cars, but we have gone as far as justice and fairness warrant in making it a crime to do certain things when motoring on the public highways.
For the information of my hon. friend I may say that the law has been severely applied, I have been sorry many times to be compelled to refuse requests and applications made by members of the house either to reduce sentences or to restore licences which have been taken away from persons convicted of these crimes. I was sorry to have to do that, but there has not been one case in which I have intervened to give back a licence that was revoked by the magistrate. I do not think my hon. friend is quite fair in saying that we are not doing all that can be done, but I am quite willing to consider his request that we should continue to look into the matter during the recess, and if the law can be improved in any way I shall be pleased to cooperate with my hon. friend in the matter.

speechtext:
Last year the minister said he would consider the amendments proposed in the bill I submitted. Among those was an amendment providing that persons who have caused death should not drive for two years. That has been found to work well in some of the states of the union, and I think it might be of great value here. The men who have been killed in these accidents had as much right to live as those who killed them. The section I proposed read:
Everyone is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to not more than six months' imprisonment and a fine not exceeding one hundred
dollars who, having caused the death of any person while driving an automobile or motor vehicle, thereafter drives an automobile or motor vehicle at any time during the next ensuing two years, notwithstanding that such death was not caused entirely or partially by fault of such driver.
In my opinion it takes two people to cause an accident, but surely there should be some penalty when a jury decides that an accident was sixty per cent the fault of the killer and forty per cent the fault of the man killed. I know if I killed a man I would never want to drive a car again. That is one reason I do not drive a car now; I am afraid of hurting somebody on our streets. I believe we should tighten up the laws in order to protect the people who use our highways. Would not the minister consider such an amendment?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, judging
from the number of resolutions I have received from trade unions .and other organizations in the riding I represent, it will not be popular to offer any opposition to this proposed amendment to the criminal code. Nevertheless I feel it my duty to point out two things which in the past have come to my attention in connection with matters of this kind.

I should like to make it very clear that I am most anxious and willing to subscribe to any legislation which in its final result is for the benefit of members of trade unions in general, or people who earn a living from physical labour. Having regard to this section I want to recite to the committee in general, and to the minister in charge of the bill in particular, circumstances which came to my attention eighteen months or two years ago. I shall try to be accurate in my statement of the facts.
A certain industry in Canada employing, according to my recollection, between 450 and 500 workers, had for many years what was known as a shop committee. There was no organized union in the industry, and no branch of any recognized national or international union. But each year the employees of the different departments met, a group of so many employees electing one to represent them on the shop committee. Thus they had an organization of representatives of employees who periodically, either four or six times a year, met with the management, discussed labour problems and complaints or other matters which the employees thought worthy of consideration. Over a period of nine or ten years this procedure had worked out very well, and there had never been labour trouble of any kind in the plant. Apparently the employees were happy and satisfied.
At the time of the intrusion in Canada of the unions of the Committee for Industrial Organization a committee of two or three walked into the manager's office one day and said, "We are officers of Union No.-" so and so "-of the Committee for Industrial Organization which has been organized in your plant, and we demand that we be recognized as the representatives of the employees of this plant." They laid upon the table certain demands for changes they desired in connection with working conditions, wages, or matters of that kind. The manager said, "Oh, no, you do not represent this plant; we have a shop committee. I have not heard from the shop committee; we have had no complaint from them." The manager sent for the shop committee and, as the result of a talk he had with them, he did something rather unusual, something which, in the vernacular, might be described as taking the bull by the horns. The next morning, as each employee came to the plant and approached one of the entrances, he was confronted with a ballot box and a ballot, and was asked to vote then and there as to whether he wanted to be represented by his shop committee, as he had been in the last nine or ten years, or by the Committee for Industrial Organization.

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
I believe a period of fifteen minutes was given for the employee to consider the matter, but he was not permitted to enter the plant until he had cast his ballot. As a result of that procedure an overwhelming majority voted in favour of the shop committee. Thereupon the manager refused to recognize the officers of the union of the Committee for Industrial Organization or to have anything to do with them. They called a strike. About ten per cent of the employees went out on strike, and the manager promptly dismissed them. He first gave them three days to return to their jobs, and be reengaged, or failing that, he would replace them with others. Most of them were so replaced.
Let us take this specific case. The men would go to the court under this section and say, "We were fired because we went on strike, and we went on strike because we were members of a union." The sole reason for the manager or owner dismissing those men was that they belonged to a particular trade union. I cannot conceive that the majority of the representatives of the people in this house would want legislation which would create that situation.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: What would the judgment be?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
It is impossible for me to anticipate what the judgment might be. I trust I shall not be considered irreverent or disrespectful when I say that having practised law for twenty-four or twenty-five years I have seen some amazing judgments given by magistrates. I think most hon. members who are of the legal profession have had similar experiences, particularly when only a small proportion of the magistrates have legally trained minds, quite apart from their being qualified as lawyers.
I know the minister is honestly endeavouring by this legislation to meet a difficult situation, and I simply point out this specific example and ask the minister and his officials to give serious consideration to the question whether there should not be some further change in the wording of this section. I acknowledge the difficulty in meeting the situation.
There is another aspect of the matter to which I should like to refer. It frequently happens that there are two unions in the same plant. One group of men may belong to union A while another group may belong to union B.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Craft unions.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
It does not matter what kind of union it is. I see my hon. friend's
point; men may belong to different unions in a plant where different craftsmen are employed -there may be one craft union and a general union. But let us call them union A and union B. One union becomes much stronger numerically than the other. We all know the struggle which has been made for years by the unions to obtain what they term a closed shop; in other words, they want to impose upon the owner or the proprietor the obligation that he shall not employ anyone who is not a member of a particular union. That situation was not so bad in the days when there was only one union, but where you have two unions in a plant and one becomes more powerful than the other, the more powerful one may go to the management and say, "Unless you make this a closed shop so far as our union is concerned and employ only our members, we will call a strike." That manufacturer or industrialist may have no quarrel with his employees as to wages or hours of labour, but in such a case the sole point at issue is that he shall be required to employ only the members of the one particular union. If that employer complies with such a demand, he is committing a breach of this section, because he would be dismissing employees for belonging to a union.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Not for belonging to a union.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Because they do not belong to a particular union. That will serve my purposes just as well. I do not think we should say by legislation to any worker in this country, "You must belong to a certain union " or " you must belong to a union."

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: This section does not touch that.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think it touches it, very clearly. My learned friend and I have disagreed before on the interpretation of the law, but I think the last occasion on which that occurred I happened to have in mind the case which decided the point I was alleging, and was able to cite it immediately. At the moment I have not such a ease available. If my hon. friend disagrees with me, he can state his position later.
As I interpret this section, if the situation which I have just outlined arose, the owner would be in an extremely difficult position. I was wondering if there would be any possibility of meeting this difficulty by including one or two words in the section to make it an offence to dismiss an employee solely because he belongs to a union or because he does not belong to a union. In other words,
Criminal Code-Trade Unions

I think you could cure the situation I have outlined by having the section read:
. . . refuses to employ or dismisses from his employment any person for the sole reason that such person is or is not a member of a lawful trade union. . . .

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
As I have been interested in legislation along these lines, I should like to congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) upon introducing this bill. While perhaps it does not go as far as a similar bill which I introduced, it does go a long way toward meeting the situation now existing in Canada. I have received a large number of messages from trade unions all over the country. As was stated during the debate on Bill No. 5, the official organizations of labour have endorsed and indeed have for a number of years asked for legislation of this kind. I can assure the minister of the appreciation of a very large number of trade unionists throughout the country.
A few days ago I happened to be reading a brief outline of trade unioD history published by the Department of Labour. It seems to me that this is simply another step in a long series of steps by which labour has tried to secure something like its rights. In Great Britain in 1799 and 1800 parliament enacted the combination acts. That was at a time when industry was organizing and labour was being placed very much at a disadvantage. It was claimed then that there was equality of treatment before the law, since the employer also came under the combination acts. As I listened to the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) it seemed to me that in his thinking he was back in the days of 1799 and 1800. Anatole France rather laughed at this idea of equality as between employer and employee, or as between one class of the community and another, when he said:
The law in the majesty of its equality alike forbids rich and poor to sleep on park benches.
Thus showing, as the Labour department paper points out, that identical treatment is not always equitable treatment. The combination acts were repealed in 1824. Then we had in 1834 the formation under the influence of Robert Owen of the Grand National Consolidated Trades Union. At this time also came the difficulties encountered by the first agricultural labourers' union which had been organized in Tolpuddle in Dorset. There followed the Chartist movement. I am touching on just a few points in the trade union movement. Then an act in Great Britain gave legal status to trade unionism in 1871.
In Canada a Nova Scotia act in 1816 prohibited combinations and referred to the numbers of working men of Halifax and other

parts of the province who "by unlawful meetings and combinations endeavoured to regulate the rate of wages." I am not going over that history in any detail. I want simply to point out that it has been a long struggle extending over many decades to secure for trade unionism anything like its rights. I wish I had time to answer from the trade union standpoint the argument, if such it may be called, of the hon. member for York South, who instanced the case of a shop committee, a company union, you might call it, where the management is supreme and the men are called together in a fashion that did not give them any real power.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: You go and talk to the men and you will find them satisfied.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I have talked with them. I know the trade union movement fairly well.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: But go and talk with the men in that plant.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Men in individual plants may be satisfied, but I submit that we cannot found legislation on exceptional cases; it cannot be done. The men have the right to organize just as much as the company. Merely because an association of gentlemen get together and agree to go into a partnership, without any legal basis, is no reason for carrying on business generally in that way. I think the hon. member for York South will admit that business generally cannot be carried on without legal documents or contracts simply because in one instance three or four gentlemen voluntarily enter into an agreement to carry on their business in a certain way. We have gone beyond that stage. The hon. member for York South mentioned an instance in which men were forced to cast ballots in a certain way, and as the management dictated, or be dismissed.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I did not say they were required to cast ballots in a certain way and as the management dictated. They cast their ballots as they wanted to; that is all.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should have altered the order of my clauses. What I meant was that in a perfectly arbitrary fashion they were required to cast their ballots. If you are going to have anything like real freedom and real justice you cannot have the men treated in that way. The very case instanced by the hon. member for York South is about the best illustration one could get to show the need of some such protection for the workers such as I hope this legislation will afford.

Criminal Code-Trade Unions

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: My hon. friend's associates compelled me arbitrarily to cast a ballot last night on five minutes' notice-a public ballot for all the world to know.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: But the hon. member voted the way he wanted to, didn't he?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Of course I did; so did the men.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: That "ballot" last night was cast in accordance with the generally accepted rules and regulations.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: And after long discussion.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: After long discussion. It was not forced arbitrarily on individuals who had no right to speak for themselves. and no right to sit in the house the next day if they voted contrary to what was considered proper. I do not think impossible illustrations of that kind should be dragged in.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: It was a secret ballot.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Even if it was a secret ballot, that does not alter the situation. My point is that it was a perfectly arbitrary mode of procedure on the part of the employer. The employees should have the right to conduct their affairs in an orderly, sensible, self-respecting way. I frankly recognize that undoubtedly there are difficulties when there are several unions in the field. There are difficulties that face labour men themselves owing to the development of industry. They have to determine whether an organization shall be a craft organization or an industrial organization, whether or not the headquarters shall be in Canada and the union a national one, or whether, as is the case with many industrial companies, it shall be an international organization with headquarters perhaps across the border. These are problems to be worked out. But that does not touch the main question at issue here. The main issue is that labour people just as other members of the community, shall have the right to organize for their own special purposes. Industrialists have the right to organize for their purposes; why not labour?
I received a letter a few days ago from a trade union official from which I should like to read a sentence or two:
There is no doubt Canadian workers should be encouraged to respect our democratic institutions, and the best way to do that is to give them a fair wage, fair working conditions, and a fair security for their dependents, also a definite feeling of better prospects and understanding with their employers.
I think that is really what the ordinary working man wants. He believes in our democratic institutions; he wants to live under
our democratic institutions. But if we are to have real democracy in the industrial field we must provide some machinery through which democracy will work. I do not think it is possible to separate political democracy from industrial democracy. The one runs into the other, and I warn the house that if we deny industrial democracy to any large group of people we are in reality endangering our own political democratic institutions. I do not think that can be put too strongly. If you are to have a law-abiding population that will refuse to take matters into their own hands and get what they want by force, then you must provide machinery through which they can work and obtain their legitimate rights.
I take it that more and more we are coming to the place where industry cannot be said to belong only to the man who owns the capital invested in it. The idea apparently held by the hon. member for York South is surely out of date. An industry does not belong alone to the capitalist or to the management. The employees have a vital interest in it, and should have their place in the management of the industry; and I believe that we are rapidly coming to a recognition of this position. If the employees are to have that share in industry, and their liberty in a field where liberty counts perhaps for even more than it does in the political field, the workers must have the full right to organize their fellow workers and must have a voice as to the conditions under which they shall work.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Is there not a difficulty in
determining where the liberty of one ends and the liberty of the other begins?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Always. That is
the very essence of government.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am talking of industrial
liberty.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Quite so, but until such time as we have something very near to socialism in this country we shall have to leave this matter largely in the hands of the workers themselves.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Do you think that would
cure it?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I think they will have to work it out for themselves, and I believe they can be trusted. The trouble as I understand it is that we do not really believe in democracy.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: We do.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Then we do not practise it.
Criminal Code-Trade Unions

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: We practise it here much better than they do in Russia.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Quite so. I do not know why the hon. gentleman should introduce Russia into this discussion.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I will tell the hon. member. It is because a system has been introduced there by the workers themselves, and my hon. friend suggests that if labour were left to adjust these difficulties they would be ironed out. It does not seem to me that I would relish the way they have been ironed out by the labour classes in Russia.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I quite agree,
because I do not believe that in Russia they have, either in the political or in the industrial field, what we would call democracy.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I agree.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: But there are other countries which have proceeded farther along these lines than we have. Take the Scandinavian countries. They have found that in the working out of their democracy three or four things must go hand in hand. They have their cooperative organizations, their trade union organizations, their own kind of political organization, and perhaps above all a generally educated public assisted along lines of what we call adult education. It seems to me we too must work along those lines if we would have in this country a thoroughly educated people capable of carrying on democratic institutions. In the meanwhile, if we really believe in democracy, we shall have to leave organization in the industrial field very largely in the hands of the workers themselves.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: As regards collective bargaining.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, as regards collective bargaining.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman says that we do not really believe in democracy, may I ask of whom is he speaking?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I am speaking at the moment of the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: And of the group for which the hon. member is speaking?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I was not thinking in political terms. I would say that we as Canadians-perhaps if we had to narrow it down, I would say, we as a parliament-do not really trust the people. It is in that sense that I use the word "we." Generally speaking we do not trust the people. We are inclined to impose something on them. I am talking at the moment merely about

trade union activities, collective' bargaining and that sort of thing. I think that to a large extent we must leave the working out of these matters to the trade unions themselves. I quite agree that if the unions were to resort to force to compel people to come in, the law would have to step in, as it would in dealing with rival concerns if two merchants came to a clash on the street.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Or the sit-down strike, for instance?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Well, a sit-down strike is caused only because the existing machinery is not sufficient to enable the parties to settle their differences in the proper way. If we are to avoid sit-down strikes or appeals to force we shall have to set up machinery through which the various groups can work in a constructive way. Then the process will be an orderly one. But if we allow things to continue so that, when an employee wants to join with his fellows, a big corporation can dictate to him whether or not he shall do it, and can even put him out of employment, democracy has no opportunity of functioning.
I had not intended to say so much this afternoon, but when I think of the way big United States corporations have come- into northern Manitoba, northern Saskatchewan, and northern British Columbia, and I believe the same is true to a certain extent of Ontario and Quebec, and proceed to erect a state within a state, and dictate to their employees how they are to live, how they are to organize, even how they are to vote, it seems to me that democracy becomes a farce. That is the situation with which we are faced in Canada. Surely we should protect the workman's right to be a free man and to carry on as a free man. That is all this legislation asks for.
On some occasion I should like to ask the Minister of Justice what effect certain limiting words may have-in the second line "wrongfully and without lawful authority"; later I notice the adjective "lawful" trade unions, "lawful" association, "lawful" right. To whose authority does that refer, dominion authority or provincial authority? I am a little in doubt as to what is meant, what lies behind and what will be the legal effect of these terms.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Before the minister replies, may I be permitted a few minutes? The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has endeavoured to turn my statement, with respect to difficulties I saw in the way of this section, into an effort on my part to oppose the organization

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
of workmen into unions, or collective bargaining, or anything of that kind. I wish to make it very clear that I have always supported collective bargaining; I have always been and .always shall be willing to support any legislation which gives to the labouring man every possible opportunity of organization. That is not the point in connection with this particular legislation. I was trying to point out that I agreed with the section in the principle which I believe it seeks to accomplish, but that the wording of it should have further consideration lest it create an evil which I believe we do not want to create. May I say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, so that he may have some regard for my sincerity in connection with the principles I have just enunciated, and so that he may not carry through life the notion that I have the trade union ideas of 1700 and 1800, that long before the days when he had an active interest in trade unionism, at a time when his main objective was leading the souls of men to eternal life, I was learning trade unionism at my parents' knees from my earliest years until 1911. Because it so happened that my father was not only a union man but president of a union, I know something of trade unionism and something of the problems of labour. I am most anxious to help in every possible way labour organization, but I still say that if this section as it now stands is carried it will lead, I fear, to inequities which in their final results will only cause its repeal, and so will not effect the purpose which the hon. member so sincerely, I believe, desires to accomplish.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am very happy to support this resolution. It 'backs up what I have been saying about the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), that he is in favour of men organizing and being protected in their labour organization. I know- of organizations and companies the heads of which understand how to treat their workers. I could name a number, but for my own protection perhaps I had better not do so. Those companies and their superintendents know how to treat their men; the officers go out with them in the summer and they have a social time with them in the winter. But I know the other kind, too. If there is any law which is true in nature it is the law of struggle, and trade unionism is no exception to that law. I have seen men scared in their shoes when they were asked to join a union. I know that because they worked with me and I had something to do with their employment. They were afraid lest they lose their jobs or get a cut in their wages. I congratulate the minister upon
bringing in this legislation at this time; for if he had received, as perhaps he has, letters similar to those which I have received since I supported this year Bill No. 5, with respect to refusal to employ or dismissal of employees for belonging to trade unions, and a corresponding one previously, it would cheer his heart to read them. At the head of the lakes I know of a group of people who would allow their superintendents to organize, but these superintendents would not allow their workers to organize. That is not fair. I know, too, that not all craft union leaders are unselfish. To my mind, craft unions do not go all the way. I have known of plants that have been thoroughly organized and people were working in those plants for 35 cents an hour. We need all the men organized, because a man who has a wife and family and has to live on 35 cents an hour becomes discontented if he finds that in the same plant there are men getting $2 an hour.
I commend the minister heartily for his progressive legislation. This to me is one of the commendable measures introduced in this house. I defy the Globe and Mail to leave blank the little space headed " What has Parliament done?" They should insert this: " Protected the right of men to organize and be protected in their organization." I hope the day will come when Christianity will have its full power in all organizations of labour and of those who employ labour; when the superintendents of corporations and the presidents of labour unions will confer together, and the superintendents will try to find out, just like the provincial or dominion whips, where there might be discontent and then in a fine way seek to alleviate it in constructive fashion. When labour and capital get together and cooperate for each other's good, legislation such as this will not be necessary, but as things are to-day it is essential and has my full support.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
My reason for rising to
say a word on this subject is an unusual one. I am going to say a word for the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson). I think my leader, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre misconstrued the motives of the hon. member. As is not unusual with a lawyer, he examines the wording and construction of a bill for loopholes, and makes suggestions as to how they may be overcome. However I doubt whether some of his suggestions would be helpful. If I understood him rightly he said the bill should be amended by adding some such words as "who is-or is not-a member of a lawful trade union." Under those words I think an employer would have
Criminal Code-Trade Unions

to continue in his employ a person who is a member of an unlawful trade union, if there is such a thing, and could not dismiss him.
I can visualize such an hypothetical case as the one he first mentioned-that is, where there might be a break from the established trade union and a new one set up, the conditions that he mentioned might arise. But I do feel that if so, a judge hearing the case would, and justly too, make his decision so that all the employees could be in the trade union in which the majority of the employees were at the time. I think that is the situation now in the United States, where they can take a poll as to which organization has the largest number of members in a particular industry, and the union with the largest membership becomes the recognized union, I doubt very much if any great difficulty will arise bec'ause of such contingencies, and if it does, I presume we shall have to do as we always do, provide for it when it comes.
I can speak in this matter only as a trade unionist. I have been a trade unionist now for almost thirty years, and I have to look at this bill from the trade unionist point of view. I cannot look at it from a lawyer's point of view because I have not had a lawyer's training. But I know from my association with trade unionists that the trade unionist, like the rest of mankind, or all the animal world if you like, is a conservative animal. He does not want to disturb the conditions under which he gets his livelihood if they are at all reasonable.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
All Conservatives are
reasonable.
Mr, MARTIN:	Did the hon. member say
all Conservatives are reasonable?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I did.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I may tell the hon, member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) that I did not refer to the Conservatives to my right. I referred to conservatives in another sense.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
What
about the Tories across the way?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I never use that word.
I was saying that trade unionists are reasonable people. They do not want to have the conditions under which they work disturbed in such a manner as to interfere with their livelihood. They want to carry on with their everyday work; it is very difficult to get trade unionists to act when there is not an essential grievance in which they are vitally concerned. I know because I have been in a number of struggles with them.

I am satisfied that this bill when- it becomes law will do a great deal to improve the harmony between workers and employers, as all the legislation referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has done down through the years.
Just one other point. I wish it might not continually happen that when we on this side refer to certain things someone opposite jumps up and says, "What about Russia?" Whether we like what the Russian people did at the time of the revolution or not, we must realize that they did the only thing they knew how to do, because they had not been taught before, by their rulers, to do differently. A people who lived for centuries under an autocracy as did the Russian workers could not possibly do otherwise, and it will take years of training in democratic procedure before they come to realize the necessity of the democratic method, if they are to make the best of themselves and get the best results for themselves in the administration of their affairs. They now adopt democratic procedure in some of their affairs, just as democratic as any other people, and they have autocracy in other parts; but the latter is the legacy they carried over from the old czarist regime. I wish hon. members would keep that in mind. If we are to have orderly development let us have it step by step, so that we shall not have changes come all at once and the same things happen as happened in Russia.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: It will be noted that in paragraph (a) of section 11 the language is "refuses to employ or dismisses from his employment any person for the sole reason that such person is a member of a lawful trade union or of a lawful association or combination of workmen." Could the minister indicate what present legal or constitutional interpretation there is of the terms "lawful trade union" or "lawful association"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: This, as in the case of other words in this section, is for the purpose of ensuring that the section will be held valid and within the jurisdiction of this parliament. As my hon. friend knows, in a general way relations between employers and employees and labour matters in general are under provincial jurisdiction, and if in any province there was anything that provided that a certain union was not lawful in that province, of course this clause would not apply.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think the minister has made it clear, but there is no federal jurisdiction and no statutory definition of what is a labour union?

Criminal Code-Trade Unions

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: No; all unions are lawful, provided they are in accordance with the laws of the land.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to say just a word or two in regard to this matter. I think we ought to keep in mind the fact that the trade union movement is peculiar to democratic countries. If we look over the world to-day we note that in all totalitarian countries trade unions have been abolished. Employees are not at liberty to form associations or gather together for their own purposes in unions of any kind. Therefore in countries such as Canada, the United States, Great Britain and France, the trade union over a long period of years has grown up as an institution within a democracy for the purpose of promoting the interests of the workers. With this I am entirely in accord. I think the time is past when any thoughtful person in a democratic state would question the value to the state, to the community and to society of a trade union. I do, however, dislike introducing into the criminal code matters which might be dealt with in other ways. Unfortunately in Canada, with our divided jurisdiction, we are frequently compelled to deal in the criminal code with a grievance or a circumstance such as that with which we are faced here, because it is the only source of jurisdiction. I have given a good deal of thought to this subject, hoping that there might be some way in which it could be dealt with other than by means of the criminal code, but I must confess that I have not been able to think of any other way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: It would have to be dealt with by the provinces.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
That was my conclusion, based upon advice from the Minister of Justice and others learned in the law. But having come to this conclusion I am forced to the view that we owe it to legitimate aggregations of workers that they shall be entitled to the protection of society to exactly the same degree that associations of employers are entitled to that protection. Obviously in a country like Canada we cannot tolerate a condition in which men are forced under duress to give up an otherwise lawful association. If such a condition obtains we must provide against it, and I understand that it has obtained; there has been definite information to the effect that it still obtains, in some instances. Therefore this legislation has been introduced, and, much as I dislike dealing with questions of this kind through the criminal code, I will support this amendment because I believe in the fundamental and
underlying right of workers, as of others, to associate themselves together for the protection of their interests and their welfare.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) upon the success that has attended his efforts, and I should like also to commend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) for bringing in this amendment. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) referred to the fundamental right of workers and others to organize. I think that is the justification for dominion intervention in a matter of this sort, and I believe that would be sufficient to give the dominion jurisdiction if it did not otherwise have it. There are certain fundamental rights such as the right of free speech, the right of free assembly, and the right of free association, that belong to the whole of Canada. They do not belong exclusively to any one province. These are fundamental rights underlying the whole Canadian constitution; I think it is the duty of parliament to see that the fundamental right of free association is protected to the fullest possible extent. I am very glad indeed to commend this legislation.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: This section has been found necessary by the minister in view of the existing state of affairs, but the general principle contained in this section, that of trade unionism and its right to function, has been in the code for nearly thirty years. This amendment is merely an attempt to bring the labour union legislation up to date and interpret it. Since when has it become a crime in this country to belong to a labour union? The Conservative party has always been a labour union party.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen may smile, but in Ontario the Conservative party introduced the workmen's compensation act. Our party believes in the protection of both the worker and the employer. Yesterday I referred to one industry in Canada which, as the result of one invention, has been able to get along with 4,746 fewer employees than it formerly required, thus reducing its pay-roll by over three and a half million dollars. Surely protection should be reciprocal; it should be for employer and employee alike. Fifty-one per cent of the people of Canada are engaged in industrial pursuits. Ninety-five per cent of our manufacturers are loyal, patriotic citizens who lead in social and patriotic work, and who in spite of heavy taxation burdens, artificial barriers and restraints to trade put on them by legislation, have striven as best they might to carry on.

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
I have consulted some of these gentlemen, many of whom have no objection to the principle contained in this section.
Previously I have referred to the proceedings before the committee of inquiry at Washington in 1927 with regard to the very principle contained in section 11. In the United States, according to the Couzens report, it was found that senior employees were being laid off at the age of forty-five; they were being turned adrift in the world. That committee dealt with the very principle contained in this section, and it took evidence from all over the world for a period of weeks and months. This senate Couzens report, which was adopted in 1927, contained these words as to protection for senior employees:
Many of them are still in the prime of life and are able to meet the requirements of industry. They are not old in the sense that they have outgrown their usefulness. Yet once they have been discharged they find it exceedingly difficult to secure new employment. It is the duty of American industry to keep these men on their payrolls rather than to turn them adrift upon a labour market which refuses to absorb their services.
I know some few of the industries in Toronto and elsewhere, and I can tell you this: They tell these men they are forty-five and that they have no work for them, but the real reason for laying them off is that the men wanted to or did belong to a labour union under the old trade union system. Just read Green's history of England to see how membership in these great trade unions spread in England, from the time of the Shaftesbury report of 1847 to 1938. Then there has been wise labour legislation by the Chamberlain government.
We are getting behind in our legislation for the protection of some of the workers in Canada. The Stevens commission did more for the workers in Canada of that day, even if it did cost $300,000, than has any other agency since confederation. The Conservative party has always been a labour party. It was the party that started the cry for cheap light and power, and cheaper fares so that the worker would not be charged large sums of money for such services. This legislation was started in England. What was the result of similar legislation in England for the workers? A general strike was prevented in England and a civil war avoided by wise labour legislation and insurance In the present world crisis two and a half million men voted for rearmament at Norwich. In the old land they have not had a civil war in a hundred years. Why does that condition exist over there? Because of England's industrial reforms. Right Hon. Ernest Brown, the able Minister

of Labour in the Chamberlain cabinet has been responsible for sensible, modern labour legislation to cure some abuses. He has brought about legislation for the benefit of those whom Disraeli called the suffering millions.
What is the policy of the industrialists of Canada? I have carefully looked into it. I believe the principle of the legislation now under consideration has been before the house for many years. If I remember correctly, my late leader last year supported the principle of a similar measure. I am going to support any wise and sensible legislation, no matter where it comes from in this house, whether it is introduced by the government, by the opposition, by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, or by others. If it is for the benefit of public rights or of the worker or the toiler in this country I will support it. I have always supported any reasonable, sensible labour legislation.
This clause has been found to be most useful in aiding employment. We have seen the reports of the Minister of Labour in connection with employment and it will be realized that this clause will be beneficial. I should like to read what I said on a former occasion with respect to the way in which five per cent of industrialists treat their senior employees. They say to them, "If you join a trade union you will have to get off the payroll." The real reason is that the employees are no longer wanted because they are over forty-five years of age. Two years ago I said this:
Senior employees, whose lifeblood has been drawn from them by long years of faithful service, are in many cases cast out without retiring allowance to make room for younger and cheaper people. It matters not what suffering is entailed for human beings so long as the stockholders are paid their dividends. This amazing selfishness and shortsightedness of the modem industrial system is creating a progressively lower standard of living and a vicious struggle for existence philosophy on the part. of the people, increasingly serious social problems which must find their tragic solution either in war or in revolution. In the face of modem methods of competitive living the royal law of love, bear ye one another's burdens and so fulfil the law of Christ, is a hollow mockery in Canada, presumably a Christian country. This is the contradiction of modern life: a truly wonderful appreciation of the value of the single soul in some quarters, but an absolute denial of any such value in others.
From the experience of the Purvis commission, the Couzens commission and the Chamberlain government, and from the experience of the Minister of Labour in the old country, who has not only supported legislation of this kind, but has imposed heavy penalties on some of the five per cent of industrialists

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
to whom I have referred, and because of the manner in which some in Canada have treated white-collar workers, I believe it can be said that this clause is a proper one.
We do not hear much about this matter in the press. They do not seem to report anything that goes on-with the exception of a few

so far as I can see. They refuse to give the people the facts on all these public questions. The people do not get all the facts. If they got the real facts of what is going on here, if they knew the way in which, for example, senior employees of forty-five years of age were being treated in some industries, if they knew that those men were being put out on the street through the evils of the system, they would say it is high time for this high court of parliament to do something. to act and aid employment and provide work for all.
I have always supported trade union movements. Municipalities have led in support of them, and in their contracts they have the fair wage clause and other provisions to help protect Canadian workers. Labour is respected by the public utilities in the municipalities in Canada.
This should be a salutary lesson for industrialists who have been enjoying high protection. I believe in real up-to-date protection for all the people all the time, not for just some of them some of the time. Five per cent of the industrialists, that portion to which I have referred, want to reap all the benefits of protection for themselves, and they are the greatest enemy a system of protection can have in any country. They abuse the privileges of a tariff system and deny privileges to their employees; they do not let the employees share in it as they should in a fair and just way, in order that the workers may live.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Unfortunately I was out of the chamber for some time and it has not been possible for me to speak until now. If I heard correctly I believe this clause is an incorporation in the criminal code of the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). I supported that suggestion at the time it was up for discussion in the house, and I wish to add only a few' words at this time.
It seems to me this is a time when industry may show its advanced ideas for the purpose of preserving the very system in which industry generally believes. The difficulty seems to me to be in the fact that there is in industry a small minority-I do not think there is a majority-which is thoughtless in its treatment of the worker. Seven or eight
years ago, on the first occasion on which I ever expressed an opinion in the matter, I said the time had come when industry during depressed times must not take the attitude of guarding its machines and plants and putting on watchmen to ensure the safety of only the inanimate part of the industry, but should include also the human element, which is more important than all the rest put together. I still think the wise industrialist insists on that.
The clause before us is along the same lines, and carries the same principle a little farther. After all it is not more than about seventy years since it was a crime in the advanced country of England to support or belong to a trade union. I wish merely to say I think the great advances which have been made along these lines in England have saved that country from many of the troubles some of the continental countries have had.
If we are to preserve-as it is my desire to preserve-the economic and democratic systems which we have, we must put into force such advanced legislation as this. Therefore I believe the Minister of Justice was wise in adopting the proposal of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and I heartily endorse the principle behind the clause.
May I say only one word about the phraseology, which, I presume, is well thought out. I was wondering how an employer might be found guilty of refusing to employ any person for the sole reason that such person belonged to a trade union. I mean that an employer might be accused unjustly, it seems to me, under that phraseology. I presume however that the law officers and the minister have gone into the matter and have decided that this is the wisest phraseology. Having that in mind I do not wish to argue about it, because I realize it is a legal matter. It just struck me as something which might be difficult to prove or disprove. However, so far as I am concerned I wholly support the principle behind the proposed legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Obviously this section meets with the approval of all hon. members in the committee. I may say the drafting of the clause was difficult. The difficulty arose in framing it in such a way as to permit its being upheld by the courts. We had it in mind also to frame it in such a manner that it would not result in unfairness or injustice to anybody. That is why certain words, which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsw'orth) has mentioned, such as "wrongfully and without lawful authority'' have been inserted in the section.

Criminal Code-Trade Unions

I agree with the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) that it is not desirable to use the criminal code for all sorts of purposes, especially in connection with matters which are rather within provincial jurisdiction. When the bill proposed last year by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was being discussed, I referred to the decision of the privy council in connection with the Insurance Act of 1917, and I quoted the words of Chief Justice Duff, who sat on that case. I quote them again:
. . . their lordships think it is no longer open to dispute that the parliament of Canada cannot, by purporting to create penal sanctions under section 91, head 27, appropriate to itself exclusively a field of jurisdiction in which, apart from such a procedure, it could exert no legal authority, and that if, when examined as a whole, legislation in form criminal is found, in aspects and for purposes exclusively within the provincial sphere, to deal with matters committed to the provinces, it cannot be upheld as valid.
That is what made the matter difficult. There is no doubt that matters concerning labour are provincial in scope. The provinces have to do with hours of labour, wages and relations between employers and employees. I was afraid that the bill presented last year could be challenged successfully by any employer against whom proceedings might be taken. As the committee knows,, employers would have the means to go through all the courts. It is desirable that legislation should be proof against the possibility of adverse judgment by the courts. The trade union officers realize that and they have applied to all the provinces to do what my hon. friend recommended should be done by this parliament. As my hon. friend said last year, and as the trade unions stated in their brief presented to the Rowell commission, the trade unions want the federal parliament to supplement the provincial legislation and take a stand as to the validity of labour unions and the right of labour to belong to a union.
Last year I gave a list of the provinces which had adopted legislation making it unlawful for an employer to dismiss an employee because he was a member of a union. Practically all the provinces have now adopted legislation which entitles us to pass this implementing legislation. In spite of what the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) said, the province of Ontario has no legislation of this kind. However, I am happy to see in the press that a bill has been presented. If it is accepted by the Ontario government, there will then be no province in which the act of an employer in dismissing an employee for membership in a labour union will not be considered unlawful. In Quebec the fair wage

act, chapter 50 of the statutes of 1937, and another act, chapter 49, respecting workmen's wages, deal with this question. It is specially stated that whoever prevents by threats or otherwise an employee from becoming a member of an association, and so forth, or who makes an attempt upon the freedom of an employee by dismissing him because he is a member of an association, commits an unlawful act.
I am sure, and it is the opinion of the officers in the Department of Justice, the legislation of the various provinces being with what it is to-day, that parliament has the right to pass this legislation and adopt the principle of the bill of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre merely by adding the few words which have been inserted in the section. As to the fear expressed by the hon. member for York South, I do not think he needs to worry. The section has been carefully drafted, and as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) mentioned, the word "sole" is put there for the purpose of protecting the employer who may have other reasons for dismissing an employee. An employer is committing a crime only when he dismisses an employee for the sole reason that he belongs to a labour union. I think that is protection against the situation suggested by the hon. member for York South.
In conclusion I need only say that the bill of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was discussed last year. Even this year there was almost unanimous approval, the constitutional difficulty being the only obstacle to its acceptance. I think that has been overcome, and I believe this legislation will make it clear that employees in this country have the right to belong to trade unions.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am predisposed to view this legislation with much favour. Like the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) I was a trade unionist at seventeen. I joined the textile union in the town of Valleyfield, and I presume I am still a member of a trade union, although we call it an association of teachers which is both provincial and dominion-wide in scope. Naturally I have a great deal of sympathy for labour unions and their aspirations. I feel confident that legitimate business will not oppose a provision of this nature, but I am afraid that in one respect legitimate business will view it with a question mark. For instance, more than one trade union may be operating in a particular plant or city. We have the international, we have the national, and in the province of Quebec we have the Catholic

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
trade unions; then there are the local trade unions which are confined to one shop or one city. Sometimes there is a conflict between these various unions, and the employer finds himself in this peculiar position, that after negotiating with one trade union a different trade union endeavours to come into the dispute and causes a certain amount of disruption. The presumption in this section is that that second trade union is a legitimate and recognized trade union and needs protection for its members under this clause such as the other trade union is getting. Yet the employer feels bound to give protection to the first trade union. So there is a conflict of opinion, and it is apt to lead the employer against his will into a certain amount of legal difficulty which he wishes to avoid, and to cause difficulty also within his own plant where the conflict of opinion is taking place.
As I was reading this clause I was turning over in my mind what would be my attitude as an employer if I found myself in a difficult situation of that sort, where two or three unions were endeavouring to secure membership from the workers in the plant and to force their desires on me as the employer.
I go one step further and say that sometimes labour leaders are not always discreet, not always willing to look at two sides of a question. An employee gets in a difficulty of some kind and is dismissed, we will say. Immediately he goes to his labour union and puts it before them that the sole reason for his dismissal was that he belonged to that union; he emphasizes that. The labour union discusses the matter with the employer, who tries to make the labour leader see his point of view, that dismissal was not for that reason but because of other difficulties. The question in my mind is this: If there is a prosecution, as there may be under this clause, on whom does the burden of proof rest to show that the employer has acted contrary to the law' under this section? Must the employer produce definite and absolute proof that he has not acted contrary to section 11? These are some of the points on which I have some difficulty, and which I should like to have cleared up.
So far as trade unionism is concerned, like the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), I believe that trade unionism should be fostered and developed along proper lines. I believe it is one of our best bulwarks against the advance of communism, nazism, fascism, or any other "ism" that may attempt to creep into this country, and for that reason
I welcome every opportunity to foster, develop and strengthen trade unionism in this country. At the same time I do not want to promote the possibilities of friction between employer and employee, and I should like to be assured that this clause will lead not to such friction but to a closer alignment between employer and employee.
It occurred to me as I was reading the clause that if employer and employee would only incorporate into their own personalities Christian doctrine and teaching-and I use the word Christian in the broadest sense of the term-we should not find it necessary to have a provision such as this. I am hoping, therefore, that along with this clause will go an educational program that will help to develop a better understanding between employer and employee.
I should like to have some of the points I have mentioned made a little clearer.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AIR FORCE, MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
As to
the onus of producing evidence to convict anyone under this section, the ordinary rules of law and procedure will apply, and it will be on the prosecution to prove that the accused comes under the clause.
As regards the point made by my hon. friend, where there may be different unions in the same shop, and the difficulty he anticipates therefrom, I would point out that the purpose here is to carry out what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre wanted, namely, to have the principle of the freedom of labour to organize and belong to a union recognized and sanctioned by the federal parliament. The words have been carefully selected to prevent any unfairness of the kind my hon. friend suggested. It would have to be the sole reason. If an employer has a contract with a group of workmen to employ them and he refuses to employ somebody else because of that contract, a man who was refused employment would not be refused because he belonged to another union but because of a contract involving a civil obligation on the part of the employer. I do not think there will be any such difficulty as has been suggested by my hon. friend in the application of the law'.

There is no doubt, and every hon. member knows it, that in a town where the employers are liberal in their attitude-not alwa3rs Liberal with a capital L, I am afraid, but still liberal,-

-where they want their employees to organize, and where they honour the employees' organizations there is a different spirit from that which prevails elsewhere. It happens that in my constituency there are two towns only about twelve miles apart where furniture is manufactured. In one of those towns the employers are very reasonable; they do not object to organization; they deal with a committee of their emplojmes, and the spirit of that town is one of freedom and of happiness even though the wages may not be very much better than in the other town, where one family have always predominated in the manufacturing business and have had a really mediaeval attitude towards the organization of labour- an attitude which they still retain and which gives a tone of fear to the whole community. Only two years ago, when the organized employees in the first mentioned town thought they would come in to help their fellows in the other town, they had to meet in a bam or some building on the edge of the town so that it would not come to the ears of the employers of the unorganized workers whom they had been trying to organize. And when the news got out, men with wives and families lost their jobs because they v'anted to organize. This happened in Grey-Bruee, w'hich I think, of course, is the most enlightened of constituencies. If it is true there, it must be true of many other parts of Canada. The need of legislation such as this is very great.

speechtext: I should like to say a wrord or two upon this amendment to the criminal code, if for no other reason than that it has been my privilege for a period of at least thirty years to represent labour unions in the courts of the province of Quebec. I think this amendment is a great step in advance in labour legislation, and I would offer my congratulations to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre upon having submitted this legislation to the house, and to the Minister of Justice for having so generously consented to incorporate it in the criminal code. However, speaking in all sincerity I should like to see this go a little further. It is my opinion that to a very great extent, apart from its moral effect, the section is illusory. I doubt very much whether it would be possible at the best of times to obtain a conviction under the section as it reads. Of course, as I say, the moral effect is considerable, and no doubt it will help largely in the progress to still more advanced labour legislation in the future. For example-and I throw this out only for the purpose of illustration-we who are connected in any way with labour unions know the pernicious influence which company unions have; and by the organization of a company union it would be a simple matter to thwart this entire section. But I think it is a step in advance, and I repeat my congratulations to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and to the Minister of Justice. We all realize and appreciate the great truths uttered this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in his references to the trades union movement. We all realize that within our own country there are those who have failed to respect the rights of the individual; and as the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorscra.) said, free speech a.nd free assembly are twin foundations, coupled with free association. As I say, I feel that this legislation is a step in the right direction, and I hope that in the near future we shall advance even further.
