Unemployment-Youth Training

Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour) moved the second reading of Bill No. 94, to provide for the training of young people to fit them for gainful employment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to assure the continuance of the dominion-provincial youth training program. The principle of this cooperative undertaking has already been accepted by parliament. Two years ago the supplementary estimates of the Department of Labour contained an item of $1,000,000 to be expended on training projects for unemployed young people. Last year the amount of this special appropriation was increased to $1,500,000. It is now intended to place this training program on a statutory basis and to provide for its continuance over a period of three years. The annual contribution proposed under the bill is $1,500,000, making a total allotment of $4,500,000 during the three year period.
I might say that a number of considerations impelled the government to bring forward this measure. In the first place the assurance of the continuance of this program over a period of three years will permit greater continuity in the several programs arranged in cooperation with the provinces across the country. Under the present arrangement there has been a certain amount of inconvenience arising from the fact that the contributions terminated as of March 31 each year. Occasionally this meant that the provinces were unwilling to continue courses beyond March 31 until they had some definite assurance that their allotments would be continued during the coming year. The present bill will enable the provinces themselves to make more adequate and accurate provision in their annual estimates for their part of the joint program, and it will also encourage, we believe, the establishment of special training centres more adequately equipped to meet the need. In other words, by this legislation we are creating a period of three years during which the provinces will be fully entitled to make plans covering that entire time. It will also facilitate the engagement of better personnel for instructors, placement officers, vocational guidance officers and supervisors by providing more security in their positions. Finally, it will permit greater publicity to arouse public interest and cooperation particularly in the matter of the placement of those who have received training.
I am not going to speak at any length in support of the motion for second reading
of this bill. When we are in committee I intend to place upon Hansard a record of the results obtained under the dominion-provincial youth training to date. At this time, however, I think I should point out that the proposals of the dominion-provincial youth training program were set out specifically in the recommendation which came to the government from the national employment commission, as follows:
The commission recommends the following as a basis upon which training plans should be framed:
Training projects of an occupational nature.
Short term learnership courses, not exceeding one year in duration, devised to provide theoretical training concurrent with specific employment;
Work projects incorporating reconditioning, training, and conservation features, for the purposes of restoring morale and of conserving natural resources;
Training projects of a physical nature to assist in the maintenance of health and morale pending employment.
It will be seen from an examination of these objectives that certain of these training projects look to the placement of trainees in industrial employment, but it is recommended that these projects should be supplemented by others which would provide for training in rural occupations not necessarily leading to new employment, and that other projects should look to physical reconditioning and the restoration of morale in those who may be employed on such projects.
I mention this because there is quite obviously a tendency sometimes to assess the entire results of a youth training program upon the basis of those who have received training and have been placed immediately in industrial employment. As a matter of fact, even upon that basis the results obtained under the dominion-provincial youth training program, in so far as projects which were designed to fit trainees for employment are concerned, compare most favourably with those obtained, for example, under the civilian conservation corps of the United States.
But apart from that entirely I would point out to the house that in addition to the benefits received iby trainees who have been placed in industrial employment, many thousands of young people across this country have received training in rural leadership upon plans based largely upon the Danish model, which already are producing beneficial results in the prairie provinces. Many thousands of other unemployed young people have received benefits through physical training, particularly in British Columbia and Alberta.

Unemployment-Youth Training
As a matter of fact, including all types of projects-and in that I include those designed to train unemployed young people for specific occupation and those designed to provide rural training and physical training-some 100,000 Canadian young people have come in contact with this program and within its framework have received a measure of training. That, I submit, is a foundation upon which we can build solidly for the future.
The plan as devised rests upon a cooperative basis with the provinces. I recognize that from an administrative point of view there would have been advantages had we been able to proceed entirely upon the basis of the federal government making the appropriation and carrying out the projects by itself. That, however, would have involved a duplication of educational facilities, particularly in technical education and equipment, and it would have involved the dominion government in paralleling employment services and contacts with industries which are already most intimately established in the various provinces. We have proceeded, therefore, upon the basis of dominion-provincial cooperation, and almost without exception the provinces have responded whole-heartedly to the invitation for such cooperation.
One advantage arising from that basis of cooperation in connection with these training projects has been a far greater flexibility than would otherwise have been possible. We can adjust courses to the needs of particular provinces. The procedure followed is to ask the provinces to submit to the dominion government for approval projects which will be best adapted to the conditions existing in the province making such submission. This has meant that we might have in Nova Scotia a certain set of projects which would differ materially from those carried out in British Columbia. But through an exchange of information, which I hope in the future may be arranged on some permanent basis by means of an annual conference of those engaged in the work of instruction, undoubtedly there will tend to be greater uniformity with respect to those projects which have succeeded in carrying out their objectives.
For the reasons given I move second reading of the bill and reserve such further information with respect to results obtained under dominion-provincial youth training operations until the bill is in committee.

speechtext:
But not in the house. I was going to say it was surprising to some of us who sat in the house that the remarks were greeted with applause from many quarters opposite. Since those remarks were made I have received many communications from youth across the country protesting against such remarks.
I have in my hand an envelope containing sixty or seventy letters written by a resident of the city of Hull, a young French-Canadian who came to see me the day following the remarks were made. He introduced himself to me by saying, "I am one of the "yaps," one of the "spineless youth" who do not want to work; but I just want to show you what I have done." Then he proceeded to present to me this envelope containing the voluminous correspondence he had conducted with some score or more companies in and around Ottawa and Hull, and outside them, in an endeavour to obtain work. He was acompanied by two other young men who were able to produce similar evidence of their activities. I cite this case as only typical of numberless ones which could be found not only around Ottawa and Hull, but across the whole of Canada.
The hon. member for Wellington North also referred to the fact that he had endeavoured to secure young men for farm work. He referred particularly to young men who came from the city and who virtually laughed in his face when he suggested that they go to work on the farm. In response to that statement I have received many communications. One in particular, which I hold in my hand, tells about nine or ten cases in which young men have applied for and obtained work on farms, and the treatment afforded them has been extraordinarily unfortunate. Not for a moment do I suggest that all of the young men who go to farms have received such treatment as those young men in the cases explained to me, over signatures, but I am sure the minister will realize that many of those who have been placed on farms have been subjected to treatment which cannot be considered as being other than intolerable. I mention these matters in passing because they seem to me to be important in view of the aspersions cast upon our youth which are wholly unjustified and without any foundation. In my hand I hold the report of the unemployment survey conducted by the Ottawa youth federation in the week of November 21, 1938. Dealing with the city of Ottawa, this report states:
The entire city was divided up into forty-five districts and every tenth house listed. In this
way a representative portion of the population was visited-2,283 addresses, 2,081 (90-9 per cent) of which yielded results of statistical value. Of the 9,369 persons contacted, 562 were unemployed young people between the ages of 16 and 30. Because of the prevalence of parttime employment it may be observed that even more than this number are affected by the unemployment situation.
Then on page 2 the report continues:
To notice a few rather outstanding points we see:
That the number of unemployed young people between the ages of 16 and 30 is 50 per cent greater than that of those over 30;
That there are 70 more males than females unemployed;
That the modal ages of 23 and 19 show that these individuals are not fresh from school;
That over two-thirds are native to Ottawa, and over four-fifths have lived here for 3 years or more;
That 20 per cent of the males and 30 per cent of the females have received no occupational training whatsoever;
That the average unemployed young person has been out of work for a minimum of 40 per cent of his time since leaving school;
That there is a tremendous percentage of young people 16 to 30 still at school (26 T per cent of those 16-30) who are ready at any moment to take their places in the ever increasing glut on the labour market, and are doomed to a probable 2 or 3 years of idleness.
Then further on:
Twenty-two per cent of the males and 15 per cent of the females failed to complete elementary school-an exceedingly high percentage for less than the minimum of education. Any training projects must take into consideration those individuals who come from families who cannot afford education higher than elementary school and those who are not mentally equipped for further education. All these need trade training and something a little more practical than merely high school academics.
The unemployed are too often criticized for their lack of desire to work-for their "don't care" attitude. The fact is that those who have worked for any appreciable length of time, as a general rule, never lose their desire to work. It is those who have never worked, who have never had the chance to feel independent, who gradually but surely cease to care. This is the point of greatest danger to our young people to-day, for 24-8 per cent of those unemployed between 16 and 30 have never worked. What can be done to counteract the ingrowth of an apathetic attitude?
A composite picture of the young unemployed male might well be as follows: He is 22, having left school at 16, his education incomplete. He is not adequately trained for any occupation and has been employed for but half of the six years since he left high school, much of which was only part-time work. While he may still have hope for the future, he has little to anticipate but unemployment. He is just approaching that state of mind where his unfortunate situation will cease to concern him, though it may be due to no fault of his own.
I place that portion of the report upon Hansard because I think it indicates in concise language a situation which we may consider



Unemployment-Youth Training
exists not only in Ottawa but in every city in the Dominion of Canada. That report reveals a dreadful condition, but I have another report which indicates a further dreadful condition. This is the report of the lieutenant-governor's committee on housing conditions in Toronto, published in 1934. On page 41 I read:
Effects of Bad Housing on Health and Morality
Tuberculosis.
The evil effects of bad housing on health are demonstrated most strikingly by an examination of the relation between slum conditions and tuberculosis. In Toronto, June, 1934, the number of cases of tuberculosis known to the department of public health for the seven ward divisions of poor housing was 299, or 37 per ten thousand of population. This is in contrast to an incidence of 25 per ten thousand for the four districts of good housing. The highest rate, 64 per ten thousand of population, was reached in ward 4, subdivision 3, which has the highest population density of any subdivision in the city.
On page 44 there is an article on general mortality, which reads:
Only a few further examples of the effects of housing on public health need to be given here. Dr. Chalmers, medical officer of health, Glasgow, is overwhelming in his indictment of bad housing. At a time when 60 per cent of the population lived in one or two room apartments Dr. Chalmers wrote:
"In one-roomed houses the death rate was 29-9 per 1,000.
In two-roomed houses the death rate was 16-5 per 1,000.
In three-roomed houses the death rate was 11-5 per 1,000.
In four-roomed houses the death rate was 10-8 per 1,000."
Dr. Chalmers goes on to say that "Bad housing increases the incidence of all infections, contagious and verminous conditions, of respiratory diseases, and of anaemia, debility and constitutional maladies. The worse the housing, the higher the death rate." After the reconstruction of slum areas in Edinburgh, the death rate of these areas fell from 45-5 per thousand in 1892 to 15 per thousand in 1910. Following the intensive housing program in Germany, where the bulk of the working class was formerly housed in one or two room apartments, there has been a marked drop in the general death rate.
Then on page 53 under the heading "conclusion," there is the following:
In conclusion, it is abundantly clear that bad housing is opposed to the true welfare of the community. It generates disease and increases mortality. It leads the young into delinquency and the old into crime. It breaks up family life. It throws increased financial burdens upon the taxpayer. And by the intensity of its attack upon such conditions may the social conscience of a community be judged.
I have endeavoured to present from these two reports, which are not my own words, a picture of the situation which I think we may regard as prevailing in our cities and among the youth of Canada generally. I am con-

fident that the minister is not unaware of these conditions. I am confident also he does not feel that the vote to be granted for youth training and reconditioning under this legislation is sufficient to begin to deal adequately with this great and serious national problem.

I have in my hand a brief on national youth administration, prepared by the national committee of the Canadian youth congress, which I shall read in part:
We greet with great favour the announcement that the federal government is prepared to continue the dominion-provincial youth training projects on a three-year basis.
Two general observations are essential to our criticism of the program as it has been carried on in the past. The first deals with the question of employment for youth. While approving the youth training projects, we are sensitive to the fact that work has been provided for only a small number of those trained and for a gravely small number of the total of unemployed young men and women. We are emphatically of the opinion that future development and success of a program to aid youth must lie to a much greater extent along the lines of providing employment. Training projects are essentially subsidiary to employment and programs must be designed to greatly increase employment opportunities.
Our second observation deals with the matter of administration of youth programs. At this point may rve express our very sincere appreciation of the work of Mr. R. F. Thompson, dominion supervisor of youth training and of that of his assistants in the provinces.
To which I should like to add my own word of commendation. The brief continues:

We are pleased with the disinterested manner with which he and his co-workers have sought the best course of action on behalf of youth and with which they have sought the cooperation and advice of the young people. Recognizing the greatly increased scope of activities and the impossible burden placed on a few individuals charged with their execution; and recognizing also the need for a more highly developed and comprehensive machinery for this work, we are strongly of the opinion that there should be developed a youth administration, maintaining the principle of dominion-provincial cooperation which has obtained heretofore.

A. Administration.

corps are enrolled and are subject to discipline while in those camps. That is an important consideration in the general scheme of the CCC. camps. speechtext:
When the house took recess at six o'clock I had essentially come to the conclusion of the remarks which I wished to make. I am sure the minister will appreciate that in what I had said up to that time I desired not to be destructive or provocative, that I was earnestly endeavouring to lay before him what I consider to be the extent of the problem in some of its aspects, and something of its nature-the problem of youth reestablishment and youth training. I am sure all of us must realize that as a result of the efforts which have been put forward to date by the minister under his training plan,

some good has been accomplished, and the complaint I have been making is that these efforts have not been carried forward nearly as far as they might have been, nor does the legislation proposed at the present time carry them nearly as far as they should go.
Just before I resume my seat I should like to refer hon. members to the Vocational Education Act of 1931 to which I alluded in an earlier speech. This act was designed to provide $750,000 a year for ten years for dominion-provincial cooperative efforts on behalf of vocational training. As a result of conditions in 1931, the year in which this act was passed, there was a letter written over the signature of the then deputy minister of labour, reminding the provinces that no grants would be made under this act until conditions warranted. From that day to this there have been no grants whatever.
May I draw to the attention of hon. members the sort of use to which, it appears to me, this act may be put? I have in my hand a copy of a letter received on February 11, 1939, signed by Doctor W. H. Butt, chairman of the board of education of Toronto. Attached to the letter is a brief laying out the claims which the board of education make for federal assistance to enlarge the central technical school for a particular project, namely the expansion of the teaching of the aircraft mechanics' course now being given at that school:
Since there was not sufficient space in the main building, the board of education rented a garage a few blocks from the school, with the thought that this would be a temporary arrangement. The work is still being taught in this garage.
Then again:
In addition to training the boys for work in the aircraft industry, the course fits them for positions in: fine instrument work; machine and radio servicing; transmission work.
To date slightly more than 100 boys have graduated from this four-year course, and about 90 per cent of them are employed. Most of them are working with firms engaged in aircraft work, but some have obtained positions with firms that put a premium upon a high degree of accuracy and carefulness.
Last June, 36 boys graduated from the aircraft course, and 21 of these secured employment in aircraft work. Most of the others have positions with other firms.
Then later:
It will be seen that this building will be entirely devoted to aircraft work, and will also be operated as a night school.
The cost of the building is estimated to be $155,000. The equipment will cost $25,000.
The Ontario government has agreed to pay 25 per cent of the cost of the building and the equipment.
The acquiring of the site will cost the Toronto board of education about $40,000, possibly slightly less.

Unemployment-Youth Training
I fully realize that the extension of a grant under this act to Toronto for the purpose just outlined would be reducing to brick and stone the dollars forwarded by the government to the board of education of that city, and that a precedent might be set in this regard. On the other hand, if vocational training is to be carried forward there must be an enlargement of the facilities through which that training is to be done, and perhaps it is not too far from the purpose of the act to suggest that here may be a commencement of work done under the act which may be regarded as highly constructive and most beneficial, not only in Toronto but in other places as well.
In what I have said I have simply been attempting to make in moderate terms an appeal for the youth of this country, an appeal not for the individual alone but for all future Canadians. As his excellency has reminded us, we all owe a debt to the past, and the only wray in which we can pay our debt to the past is to put the future in debt to ourselves. Not only is it incumbent upon us to regard these young Canadians as those for whom we have simultaneously a direct charge and an indirect charge at the moment, but they are the ones who will be responsible for the future of this dominion, and we should be prepared to do our part for them in equipping them not only for the lives they have to lead, but also for the contribution that they can make to this dominion. It is on their behalf and in that spirit that I have made this appeal to the minister to see if there is not some way in which he may substantially increase the program which he has at present in mind.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OP YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
As I understand the purpose of this bill, it is to put the youth training scheme, which has been in operation for the past two years, upon a more permanent basis in order that those who are planning this work may do so with some sense of stability and with some idea of continuity for the years which lie ahead. With that principle, I think, all of us will heartily agree, and it is unfortunate that more of the projects which are undertaken as relief measures were not placed on a longer term in order that those who are planning in the provinces could do so with something in mind for one or two years. Therefore, in my opinion, the idea of putting this on a three year basis is an admirable step.
The presentation of this bill gives me an opportunity to say some things about the youth training scheme which I think ought to be said. When the resolution was presented in 1936 by the hon. member for Greenwood
(Mr. Massey), I believe I spoke immediately after him and at that time corroborated what he said with reference to the need of a scheme such as has been carried on during the last two years in Canada. In common, I believe, with the other men in the house who were interested in this work, I was pleased when the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) graciously accepted the resolution in principle and the following year brought down supplementary estimates with that in mind.
We have now had two years of this scheme in operation. I suggest first to the minister that those two years have shown the inadequacy of the extent to which we are tackling this problem. As a response to a normal condition this scheme has been satisfactory, but as a response to an abnormal situation, as a response to the terrible times in which we live, this scheme, to my mind, has been inadequate, puerile and in some respects actually asinine.
Let us consider it. To begin with, it covers only a fraction of the young people in Canada who need training and guidance. The pamphlet which was issued by the Department of Labour, entitled, "Training Canada's Young Unemployed," in its tabulated dominion statistical summary of March 31, 1938, places the total number given training at 32,301 men and 23,156 women, making a total of 55,457. The minister this afternoon, however, said that there had been considerable increase; I believe he said about 100,000 young people had come within the framework of this scheme. I point out that this touches only a fraction of the problem. I point out further that even of the fraction that are touched the number who are receiving adequate training is very much less. For instance, in the same summary in the pamphlet entitled "Training Canada's Young Unemployed" issued by the Department of Labour, we find that although 55,457 young people were given training, only 14,649 finished courses designed to train for employment, and of these 3,282, or 22-4 per cent, found work. In other words, of the 55,457 who began training, only 14,649, or about 25 per cent, finished, and of the 55,457, only about 6 per cent were placed in employment.
Of course, it is easy to see why only 25 per cent finished and why such a small number were actually given training. In the first year, 1937, this parliament voted $1,000,000; and last year, $1,750,000, making a total of $2,750,000, assuming it was all spent. The minister said this afternoon that aibout
100,000	young people had come within the framework of this scheme, which means that for all purposes the average amount that could be spent per individual was $27.50,

Unemployment-Youth Training
which of course could not possibly cover instruction, training, equipment and cost of administration. Even if we assume that the provinces paid their half, it still would not provide adequate training. So what actually happens is that while we have a big figure of
100,000	young people coming within the framework of this scheme, the actual fact is that a very small percentage of these young people actually receive adequate training to enable them to be placed in industry.
I take a concrete illustration in the city in which I live. I speak subject to correction, using it merely as an illustration. The amount voted for the training of unemployed male youth, I believe $1,850, was turned over to a committee who did the very best they could with that amount of money; no criticism can be levelled at them. What happened? Of the $1,850, $1,600 went to giving a course in mechanics and electricity and welding which took in altogether about sixty-eight young men. They received a good training, I know they did. But the other $250, of course, had to do for all the rest, who were merely put into a course of gymnastics, allowed to play basketball for a couple of nights a week. They could have got that at the collegiate or with the boy scouts or a number of organizations in the city. So it does not cover the matter to say that 100,000 young people have been brought in. The number of these young people nominally associated with the scheme is out of all proportion to the number who will actually receive benefit.
To substantiate that I call attention to a statement in the Leader-Post headed:
Department control for youth training is Weyburn idea.
This is a statement made by a gentleman who was in charge of the committee for youth training in the city, certainly not critical of the government, an interested citizen. This is what he said:
Weyburn, April 3.-George F. Bell, chairman of the Weyburn committee of the dominion-provincial youth training movement, will recommend sweeping changes in the set-up of the scheme to Dr. J. G. McKechnie, deputy minister of education, he told the Leader-Post in an interview at the close of the course last week. Greater interest by farm boys.
Although he was enthusiastic about the success of all phases of the winter classes conducted in Weyburn during the past five months, Mr. Bell emphasized the fact that present division of activities between the department of education and the extension branch of the university of Saskatchewan was not satisfactory.
He felt very keenly that it did not give farm boys opportunities they were entitled to under the scheme and he believed farm boys would take greater interest in the classes than sons of urban dwellers.
IMr. T. C. Douglas.]
At the present time, funds are divided between the department of education and the university, and the department's share is used for urban training while the university portion is earmarked for rural training.
Only three weeks for farm boys.
The extension branch of the university provides a three weeks course for farm boys and the urban makes provision for a five months course. The brief three weeks course, too short to be of much benefit, according to Mr. Bell, entails additional expenditure for professors' travelling expenses because they have to go from Saskatoon to rural training centres.
The department of education should have complete charge of the youth training movement, said Mr. Bell, the university should drop out of the picture altogether, school boards should administer the scheme locally and thus remove need of setting up local committees that often had little experience in these matters.
Mr. Bell cited the case of a centre that failed to start classes on time because it was difficult to get a local committee to act. The school board there, on the other hand, could have begun the task in hand at once, Mr. Bell pointed out.
Dividing the program into urban and rural sections served only to slow up the plan and did not give all boys equal opportunity.
A total of 47 boys took advantage of the courses and there were 26 in motor mechanics, machine works and vulcanizing classes-
And twenty-one took the classes in electricity. I said a total of 68, it was really only forty-seven.
I draw that to the attention of the minister. I realize that this scheme is in the experimental stage. While I know there are some excellent men carrying on this work in Saskatchewan, while I know that in many instances they are only feeling their way, the fact remains that if this scheme is to mean anything at all, if it is to mean even a fraction of what those who brought it before the house envisaged that it might mean-I include the minister in that-then a much larger sum of money must be voted for this purpose and a different system of administration adopted,
The second thing I want to draw to the attention of the minister-I am sure it is hardly necessary-is that this bill provides for a continuance of divided jurisdiction between the dominion and provincial governments. As the minister said this afternoon, the scheme was on a cooperative basis, and under this bill it is going to continue on a cooperative basis for three more years. Last year in this house the minister made a speech in which he pointed out quite correctly the unsoundness of the principle of having one governmental body raising money and another body spending it. He pointed out the difficulty of having provincial governments carrying out projects initiated and financed by the

Unemployment-Youth Training
federal government. No one knows better than he the tremendous difficulty encountered in carrying out that kind of scheme. Of course the excuse given is that under the British North America Act we cannot do anything else. But a report of the dominion-provincial relations commission is expected this summer. It is expected that some action will be taken to bring about a clearer apportionment of jurisdiction between the provincial and federal governments, and it seems to me unwise to continue to carry on a scheme in which the federal government is putting up the money and has no direct control over the scheme which it is financing to the extent of 50 per cent. Because that is happening, the situation outlined by Mr. Bell arises.
I have in mind numbers of young men on farms, for instance. There is one young man in particular who a number of years ago went to the United States, where he took a course in electric welding. Then he was called back to the farm on account of the illness of his parents. On his farm he fixed up a shop, where he has done a great deal of electric welding for the people of that neighbourhood. Along come these courses. He wants to take the electric welding course in order to round out the work he has already done, but he is not eligible. He is eligible for an agricultural course but not for this course, while on the other hand young men who are eligible for this course are, in many instances, not interested in it at all. It seems to me the young men on farms have not had the opportunity they should have had under this scheme.
Then there has been no provision at all for the so-called white-collar unemployed youth. I refer to young men who have perhaps gone part way through university and have had to stop on account of lack of finances. They are not primarily interested in blacksmith courses or agricultural courses. No provision at all is made to provide for them the type of work for which they are trained and fitted or to permit them to go on and be further educated. So this group of young people, whose name is legion, are entirely left out under this scheme. The other night the minister made an announcement at a banquet in this city. It seems to 'be becoming a habit with this government to make most of their pronouncements at banquets. I believe this was a banquet of the Twentieth Century Liberal club, at which I understand some members of the Nineteenth Century Liberal club were in attendance as honorary guests. The minister announced that the sum of $1,000,000 was to be spent in forestry work.

During that very same week this house was discussing unemployment and the announcement was not made here, which is significant. However, that is not particularly important. The fact is that $1,000,000 is to be spent, and the minister says it will give employment to some
10,000	young men. I hope when we get into committee the minister will give some details about this scheme; how much these young men will get and what kind of camps we are going to have; whether we are going to have a return to the sort of camps that were condemned by the Prime Minister in 1935. I have in my hand a booklet entitled "Mackenzie King's Speeches to the Canadian People," published by the National Liberal Federation, Ottawa. With regard to the regime of that day the Prime Minister said:
Youths are sent to the camps.
Then he goes on with an indictment of the practice of sending young people to camps. We have a right to know, and I am sure the minister will want to tell us, what kind of camps will be set up. Some camps can be beneficial. Are these to be camps of that type? On the other hand the minister no doubt has received a brief from the national vocational corps, advocating camps. I am not going to quote extensively from it, but I think one or two paragraphs at the beginning are worthy of consideration:
January 20th, 1939.
National Vocational Corps
It is an established and well known fact that in excess of 400,000 young men are unemployed in Canada to-day, in spite of the fact that Canada is the fifth trading nation in the world. The two facts, taken together, would indicate that the unemployment of youth is not a condition that exists temporarily, but is a condition that has to be aggressively approached and handled as a permanent measure.
Due to the lack of facilities for the training of apprentices, young men are not being trained in any of the trades to an appreciable extent.
The day when Canada could rely on its isolated position as its only means of defence is past. The increase in the cruising range of aircraft has brought the shores of countries from whom we may have to defend ourselves, side by side with our own. The mineral wealth, agricultural wealth and vast spaces which we accept as part of our every-day life, appear to the over-crowded countries of Europe as a paradise to be attained at almost any cost. The young men of this country must be trained to enable them to provide, in ease of need, a

Unemployment-Youth Training
defence force sufficiently strong to retain for themselves, who are the future of Canada, the homes in which they live.
I read that to a group of single unemployed young men and' they burst out laughing. I did not realize until then how funny it was that a group of young men who had no homes and no place to sleep were to be given the privilege, according to these gentlemen, of being put in camps in order to be trained to protect the homes of somebody else. Then they go on to advocate the setting up of these camps, which would be primarily military camps and which would accommodate large groups of young men running up to
5,000	in number. I need hardly say to the minister that we do not want camps of that kind; that if camps are going to be set up in Canada, this should be done with the idea of training young men, giving them proper recreation, reconditioning them physically and, finally, placing them in industrial life so that they will not become a glut on the labour market.
I want to refer for a moment to a brief with which I know the minister is familiar, in order to draw it to the attention of the house. It is a brief on national youth administration prepared by the national committee of the Canadian youth congress and submitted to the minister on March 1, 1939. This group of young people have done some commendable work. Perhaps the most commendable thing they have done is their effort to get other young people like themselves to concentrate on thinking through their own problems and to endeavour to make constructive suggestions to those who are in positions of responsibility. While it has not always been Dossible, I am sure, to accept their sugges-,ions, the fact that they are doing some constructive thinking along these lines is an admirable sign, and these young people are to be congratulated and commended.
The program which they outline for the government with respect to Canada's young unemployed they classify under four headings: educational, placement, employment and recreational. Under the first heading they deal with the academic problem by saying:
There are large numbers of young people every year who are compelled to leave schools or colleges, due to inadequate financial resources, and who thereby swell the ranks of untrained job seekers, causing greater competition in the labour market, forcing down working standards and impoverishing the human wealth of the nation.
With that in mind they proceed to make a number of suggestions concerning national scholarships, special work projects for students and the setting up of technical training facilities. Also under the heading of education

they outline technical work that might be undertaken, such as learnership courses, apprenticeship courses and so on.
Under the second heading, placement, they outline the setting up of a vocational guidance system to take these young people who are brought within the framework of this scheme; find out what they can do apd train them along those lines for which they are best suited; give them some guidance and some direction in finding that niche in the industrial world into which they can best fit.
The third suggestion is that of employment projects. In part they say:
We recommend development of opportunities in mining, forestry, fisheries and agriculture. With specific reference to the last two mentioned, we urge that moneys be made available in the form of loans for young people desirous of establishing themselves in these fields; and these loans to be at low rates of interest, repayable over a long period of time, with reference to economic trends.
Then they go on to outline a number of schemes in the industrial field which might be taken up to give these young people some type of employment, and set them to work.
Finally, they recommend recreational projects, and say:
We have observed with enthusiasm the development in British Columbia and Alberta of the provincial recreation centres and their excellent program of physical recreation. We urge that special publicity be given to this program, with the purpose of developing a nation-wide campaign of physical fitness and the facilities for its development in all provinces.
That is a fine suggestion. Yesterday when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) was talking about needing defence equipment to defend our religion and our economic security, I could not help thinking that the best defence Canada could have is a group of young men and young women throughout the country with recreational opportunities to get out in the fresh air, get to camp and have proper diet and proper exercise. I am sure it would be appalling, if it were possible to conduct a physical examination of the young unemployed in Canada, to find how many of them are not physically in shape.
Sometimes in our smug complacency we are content to sneer at other countries. There are countries with which I and no doubt other hon. members do not agree. But when we see what countries like even Germany, Italy and Switzerland are doing for their young people by means of their strength-through-joy movement, and through summer camps, we realize that what we are doing is not very much. They are giving their young people training and opportunities to put their

Unemployment-Youth Training
bodies into shape,. We are doing comparatively little to give the underprivileged young people in Canada an opportunity to have healthy bodies, the basis of healthy and sound minds.
May I conclude my remarks by saying to the minister that I think there is presented to him a greater opportunity than is presented to any other man in Canada. He has an opportunity to make a lasting contribution to his day and generation. I am not proAmerican, but I have studied in the United States, and in the last two summers I have had opportunities to come in close contact with men who are managing some of the NYA, WPA and the CCC camps. I have had an opportunity of making observations first hand, and I say that the people in the United States, without patching up figures to make them look as though they are doing more than they are actually doing, have tackled this problem in a big way. First of all we must take notice of their 1.500 CCC camps, where their young men are not only learning something, but receiving physical training, laying aside some money, and going through a placement service which endeavours to place them successfully when they have finished their courses.
I went to a number of states, and talked not only to the young men in the camps but to the parents of young people who had gone to those camps. The parents expressed their pleasure; they were thrilled with what was being done. Under their WPA projects they have done something for classes of people whom we in Canada have totally neglected. Through their WPA they have taken young musicians, teachers and actors, and university graduates who could not find work, and have given them employment. They have set up little theatre guilds, symphony orchestras and universities for the unemployed, so that unemployed professors may teach unemployed young people. Orchestras composed of unemployed young people are going about the country putting on concerts. Other groups are putting on plays in different parts of the country. By these opportunities the administration is doing two things, it is keeping up the morale and spirit of independence of those young people, and at the same time it is making some contribution to society.
The same observations would apply to their employment projects. One could go into districts just as hard hit as the southern part of Saskatchewan, and he would see under the WPA where they have torn down old school houses and erected in their place new ones with excellent recreational facilities and the very best of equipment. They have
erected hundreds of little hospitals in towns which could not afford to build hospitals of their own. They have built good roads and have erected some of those great dams. One may see these young men working in the camps, quarrying rock to foe sent to the dams.
Here are young men who are retaining their self-respect and getting 'back the esprit de corps which will make them good citizens. In the second place it is adding to the natural assets of the great republic of the United States. One cannot begin to value that in dollars and cents. The NYA have set up scholarships whereby young people who, under normal circumstances would have had no opportunity, find it possible to go to school, a university or a technical school.
I am not suggesting that we follow that program slavishly; I am not suggesting the people across the line have not made serious mistakes. They are the first ones to admit that they have. But they are facing this problem with courage and initiative. They have taken hold of a difficult problem, one for the handling of which there are no precedents, and they have had the courage to tackle it. They are tackling it in a big way.
When I look at the situation in Canada and see that only about 6 per cent of the young people who obtain training are placed, and only about 25 per cent of the people who take training finishing that training-

Before coming specifically to what we have done, let me say that the hon. member for Weyburn has referred to what the totalitarian states of Germany and Italy have done for youth. I should have thought he would consider those two countries the last ones to look to for a solution of this problem. In 1937 the hon. member for Greenwood and I were in Rome together, and one afternoon we saw the head of the Italian state review almost half a million young men between the ages of fourteen and twenty who passed by him in an almost unending procession, wearing the uniform of the fascisti. That was how II Duce was handling this problem. That is Hitler's way of handling this problem.

I do not mind a question, but I object to a speech. The fact is that the regimentation of the unemployed in Germany and Italy is not simply a question of physical training. It is the use of the youth of those two countries for destructive purposes, which in the long run will mean destruction not only for those two countries but perhaps for our civilization. To use those two countries as an example for Canada to follow, as the hon. member for Weyburn has done, makes one wonder whether the hon. member, who parades as a democrat, has possibly not a greater love for fascism than he is prepared to admit.
I admit, Mr. Speaker, that our record is not perfect. There are many things which, in my judgment, the Minister of Labour might have done, 'but he has done a great deal, and to that extent I propose giving him credit to-night.
First of all, let us look at the problem generally. Under the Minister of Labour the following broad types of projects were undertaken. One would think from the remarks of hon. members opposite that nothing had been done.
First, work training in occupations allied to forestry and mining.
Second, urban occupational training for men and women, including assistance in training apprentices and learners in industry.

Forestry training in New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia. Woodlot cultivation in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. Surveying and prospecting in New Brunswick. There in itself is an impressive record given in a general way, indicating, as the Minister of Labour said this afternoon, that over 100,000 young people have been in one way or another affected by the program for youth rehabilitation under this government. It may not be everything; it may not be all that hon. gentlemen want, but to say that nothing has been done is to give expression to something which is not the case.
Under urban occupational classes for men and women the following were carried out: radio servicing, motor mechanics, diesel engineering, machine shop welding, painting, plastering, carpentiy and woodworking, frame house construction, electricity and house wiring, art, textile designing, commercial refreshers, dressmaking. power sewing, machine operating, waitress training, home nursing and so on.

speechtext: May I say to the Minister of Labour that unfortunately the difficulty in respect of this whole program arises out of our divided jurisdiction. Unfortunately it is not possible under the constitution for the central authority to deal with this problem in the efficient way in which I think it must ultimately be dealt with. And that situation has brought about a greater achievement in some provinces than in others. Not much rise will come of my saying that one or two provinces have failed to take advantage of the offer of the federal government, but the fact is that in at least two provinces the youth have not been given the opportunity that is accorded to youth in the other provinces. That is a situation with which, until the British North America Act is given the necessary legal refinements, we cannot adequately deal. Last fall I went to the minister of labour of Ontario-I had an interesting and, I think, a worth while conference with himto urge upon him the opportunity that this kind of assistance might give for the setting up of recreational work. The hon. member for Weyburn rather laughed at the recreational work of the youth program in some of our provinces; but our recreation suggestions are based upon the experience of the United States, and I have it on good authority, the best authority in the United States, that recreational work is regarded by the authorities there as of preeminent importance. In my own city of Windsor-and I take it as a good example of what may be done-in 1935. 1936 and part of 1937 a gentleman by the name of Angus Buchanan who had been employed by the Y.M.C.A. made a canvass of the citizens and collected a few thousand dollars. With that money, for five nights in the week several thousand young men and young women were given training in various courses of athletics, various kinds of homework, mechanical training, and so on. He was able out of the funds thus collected to give to various people who acted as instructors small honoraria. That work was commendable, and it had an important effect on the community; it took out of many homes young men who had never been in a gymnasium-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OP YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: What had the federal government to do with that?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OP YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
I am now criticising the federal government, if the hon. member will just listen. That I consider to be a worth while work. It did not give jobs, but it did provide thousands of men and women with an opportunity to use their leisure time profitably. Unfortunately, let me say in answer to the hon. member for Waterloo South, in our present circumstances it is not directly possible for this government to prescribe that this sort of work should take place. I had hoped that the government of Ontario would see fit under its powers of administration to recognize the value of this sort of work; but the policy of the government of Ontario is otherwise, and I cannot change that. I do ask the Minister of Labour, if there is any way in which it can be cultivated, to consider the importance of this recreational work.
Having mentioned the one organization, I should like to take the opportunity of mentioning work along similar lines, done by the Catholic youth organization of Windsor, utilizing the leisure time, whether the whole day or part of the day, of young men, and giving them an opportunity of learning things which under an unorganized system they would not have had. I should like to see that work carried on; it cannot be carried on endlessly by private philanthropy, and I believe

the experience of other countries in recreational work would certainly confirm our efforts along these lines.
I have spoken longer than I intended. In conclusion, may I simply say, in no political sense, but speaking as one young Canadian to a group of young Canadians who sit in this house and who represent thousands of our people, and addressing myself also to older men who, I am sure, are as much alive to this problem as we are even if they are not as close to it, that this is a great problem. Its social implications are great. The opportunities of government for dealing with it are limited. Industry, the school and all other agencies in the community can do their share. Surely it is not too much to expect that we might segregate from our political controversies this one problem and all of us try to give it the leadership it deserves, try to give to our young people some hope, some opportunity which at the present time, in so many instances they are denied. I firmly believe that the Minister of Labour and the government of this country are to be commended for the work begun, a work which, alongside the programs of other countries, is as commendable as anyone can make it appear to be.
But there is still much to do, there is still a great opportunity for the Minister of Labour, and I know that as he faces his task on the morrow he will realize, just as we all do what this problem means in the future of this country. Hon. gentlemen opposite will make a great mistake if in addressing the youth of this country, as they do and as I perhaps often do, we place the emphasis solely on the economic side of life. We have all gone through pretty much the same sort of experience; we all know that a job is an important thing; we all know that a man who is in economic want is suffering possibly one of the greatest of human needs. But life is not made up of dollars and cents only. Those who go about preaching that there is no opportunity in this country for youth are not being fair to youth or fair to Canada. There are opportunities in this country, opportunities of building a great nation. While I would be the last to deny that we must do something along the lines followed in these instruction courses, in these national scholarships, in all sorts of other programs, we should not hesitate, standing in this house or speaking in other places, to lay emphasis where emphasis is due; to say to our young men: True, our problems are great, true, the task that lies ahead of you is great, possibly unprecedently great; but for any hon. member of this house 
to say that it is hopeless as some hon. gentlemen have said outside, is to do the youth of this country the greatest possible injury.

all of Canada at least 600 or 700 fine young men could be employed. The very best of our youth go into that line of work.
If the bill covers assistance in connection with the erection and fitting of schools I believe money might well be spent in that direction. My recollection is the board of education said that of an expenditure of $40,000 they would have to pay about $20,000. If the bill covers activities of that kind it would have my support.
I also found in Washington that their scheme of sending youth to finish courses in universities, courses that they had started but not finished, or to take additional lessons after they have finished the course-sons and daughters of parents who are wholly unable to send them further, either to commence or to add to what they have already learned- was that they divided approximately 90,000 unemployed young men and women they had decided to send to the various universities of the United States on a basis of 9-3 per cent of the enrolment of each university.
From the remarks of some hon. members who have preceded me I gather the impression that they were opposed to the government, through this appropriation, giving further education in universities to the youth of our land. I am not. I am in accord with such a plan, and I would support heartily expenditure the minister may have in mind for the re-education or the completion of education, of youths in universities. I understand the government in Washington advances $15 a month to a beginner in a university and $30 a month to one who has graduated but who has returned to the university for further studies, or to perfect his education.
I do not know how the government can take care of the problem completely unless it takes care of it along many different lines. Some time ago in this building I saw pictures of forestry operations in British Columbia. Well, such operations would take care of one class of youth. Then, in line with the suggestion I made a moment ago, young men who are mechanically inclined or want to be machinists or toolmakers or craftsmen of one kind or another might be placed in plants, by the government. I am sure manufacturing plants would be glad to avail themselves of the opportunity of having such young men. If I were arranging for an industry to absorb a. number of young men either through vesti-oule school training or training under practical conditions within a plant, I would arrange for young men to stay in a plant for a sufficiently long period to learn a trade. It would not be sufficient to remain only a few months, as has been suggested. A man cannot learn 
a trade in a few months. It would require three or four years for him to receive proper training.
If I were in charge of a program of that kind I would say to industry, "Here, we will provide for you fifteen young men"-or twenty-five young men, depending on the size of the industry. I would say, "We will allow your company so much per youth a month to train these young men. So much will be allowed for each one on the understanding that when they have been trained and have graduated three years hence they will be absorbed into your business." In the meantime other men will have graduated off the map, altogether. They will have gone, for one reason or another. They may have gotten too old, or died in the meantime, or may have left the business for some reason or another. Therefore, if a permanent three year plan could be made to operate in the manner I have indicated, I am sure a good many young men could be at once placed where they would be learning something that they cannot learn at the present time.
Money has been spent in the old country along these lines. I have in mind one particular plant, a very large one, in which approximately 4,000 youth were working, and I believe they were working on some such basis as that. The government supplied so much, and the company so much. So that, as someone has said, through industry quite a number of young men can be placed in training. And, knowing as I do about the dearth in this country to-day of trained mechanics and the training of mechanics, in my judgment it would be a fine thing and a fine national investment if the federal government would take action along this line.
Someone has said something about the CCC camps. Perhaps I have visited as many of those camps as any hon. member in the house. I have covered a great number of states, and I believe I can say that I have visited fifty different CCC camps. My experience, however, has not been the same as that of other hon. members whom I have heard speak to-night. In the great majority of the camps I visited, my experiences were satisfactory. Later, on discussing the CCC camp problem with the head of the department in Washington, I was shown placement figures different from those which have been recorded to-night. I have not any late figures, so that perhaps I should not quote any percentages. Although I did not speak with the secretary himself, I did speak with the official immediately under him, the man in charge of the whole program, and he was more than pleased with the record. He told me these

young men were well trained, and I may say my observations convinced me that young men were well trained in many walks of life, although in that statement I woulc not include the industrial field about which I spoke a moment ago. However, they wen certainly well trained in civility and smartness. They were taught to use their minds, hands and feet. They were well set up. The head of the department told me there was a marked demand for these young men, and a great deal of the work of the department was taken up in placing young men trained in those CCC camps. It was acknowledged that they were much better, in many respects, than the young men on the street corners who, in many instances, were uncivil, with the result that business and industry did not wish to employ them.
I do not believe I have much more to say. I rose merely to present the ideas of one who should know something about industry and employment, and the position youth may take in industry. If I have said anything which would help the minister, or if I have said anything which would direct him along the line of encouraging industry to take in more young men, as a matter of school training, I shall be satisfied. I believe the minister, who is presented with a difficult problem, would be well advised to call together the heads of perhaps fifty large companies in Canada who would each be in a position to take on at once fifteen or twenty-five trainees. I would invite heads of labour organizations to attend and to sit round a conference table to discuss the problem as I have presented it.
Even with the adverse conditions under which it must operate to-day-I shall not say anjdhing about the causes at the present time for fear of being accused of playing politics- I am sure that industry is ready to encourage the improvement of the young men of our country. It is ready to assist the government and this country in making more pleasant the lot of these young men. No one knows better than the heads of industry how necessary it is that these young men should be trained; no one knows better than the heads of industry how necessary it is that young men to-day should receive training similar to that wdiich their fathers received. Perhaps this can be done through a system of apprenticeships and vestibule schools in industry assisted by the government, and there may have to be some guarantee by industry that these young men will be taken into the plants after they have been trained. I am sure a great number of young men could be trained, and it would all be for the best interests of this country.
