speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up much of the time of the house, but I think this is an opportunity for those who know something of the work that has been carried on to tell other hon. members what has been done. Encouragement should be given to the minister, to the ministry and to the house as a whole to continue along such lines as are being discussed this evening. I am glad to see this bill being introduced for the purpose of assisting in the training of young people to fit them for gainful employment. I assume that this is going to be worked out in two ways, or with two objectives in view. The first is to help these young people to get through a most difficult period in their lives. An effort is to be made to fit them for more useful occupation in order that they may live better, happier and more useful lives. This difficult period through which the youth of our land is passing is not entirely on account of lack of material wealth, but is aggravated by the infection which has spread from the old world to the new. This has had an effect upon the minds of many of our youth. They have had to listen to so many unsettling theories and untrue sayings that they find themselves in the difficult position of not knowing what to believe. Very often they find themselves floundering round in an unnatural way and they are not to be blamed for seeking the truth.
In my opinion one of the greatest things that could be done during the formative years of our youth is for the government and the local authorities to come along and offer these young people an opportunity of acquiring further knowledge to fit themselves to play a more active and useful part in the community. The work of this kind that has happened to come under my observation has left no doubt in my mind that it was well worthwhile. Attempts have been made to convince boys and girls that there is no place for them in the scheme of things. They do not know whether to believe the statement they hear so often, that there is no hope for them in the system under which we now operate and under which our forefathers lived for so many years. That system encouraged individualism and there was greater individual responsibility; a man was taught to hoe his own row. At times our youth do not know whether that saying still holds true. Some do not know whether they must lean on the state and must bend their wills and ambitions to the will of the state. In difficult times like these it is most encouraging to them to realize that the dominion, provincial and local authorities are

Unemployment-Youth Training
making it possible for them to acquire that wider knowledge which will make them more capable citizens.
While they are gaining that knowledge they will be in an environment which will open up a page of life that they did not know existed, a page that will reveal to them the story of the learning of the ages which their teachers are ready to pass on. During last fall I had an opportunity of visiting many districts in which short-term schools were being held. These schools were being conducted for only two weeks at a time, but valuable instruction in agricultural subjects was given by instructors from the extension department of the university of the province from which I come. Boys to the number of seventy or seventy-five gathered together for two weeks, and during the mornings, afternoons and evenings they were getting new pictures of progress in the industry in which they had spent their young days and in which the majority of them are likely to spend most of their future time. Every new lesson had its particular appeal. Instruction was given in many phases of agriculture, such as live stock breeding, and feeding, field crop cultivation, conditioning of implements, poultry-keeping and killing, bee-keeping, horticulture and other cultural activities. When these classes were being held, many of the older people attended to encourage the younger people by their presence, but in fact being helped through being able to carry away some new knowledge or to learn some new wrinkle from the teacher.
Other schools were held for longer periods to teach motor mechanics. Young men were given instruction in actual shops with tools that are in everyday use. These schools continued for three, four and sometimes five months. When the boys from the country or the town went back home after having attended one of these motor mechanic schools, they were better fitted to do the necessary work on the farms, in the forests and in other industries that demand mechanical knowledge. To-day an evolution is occurring in agriculture and newer methods are more in use than ever before. A more exact knowledge is required to-day both in agriculture and in industry, and it is well that young people should have an opportunity to fill in what would otherwise be idle time by acquiring this knowledge. I am firmly convinced that only by a deeper and sounder education can we hope to solve the problems confronting us at the present time.
There are many schemes being put before the people of the world to-day. Some of these are not sound and have led certain nations

along a most dangerous path and other nations seem likely to follow the same path. The fact that certain people seem ready to follow such a course is not due to any badness of heart of the people, but rather to a lack of knowledge and the ability to follow through to an ultimate sound conclusion. We should not be satisfied, as so many of us are at the moment, with knowing only one phase of the truth. Knowledge is the way by which we can ultimately escape from the dangers confronting us.
I should like to give a picture in a few words of some of the work that was done in youth training schools in the province from which I come. As many hon. members know, conditions have been extremely difficult in the last few years in many rural parts of Saskatchewan, although the people I represent have been more fortunate than many others in that they have had fairly good crops. But prices and other circumstances have been such that it has been difficult for them to get along as they would like to do and as they did in previous years. But in spite of conditions the enthusiasm of these people for the youth training schools was great.
Coming to one centre where a school was going to be held for a short term. I found that arrangements had been made by different organizations. One had put a large hall at the disposal of the school authorities, and another had responded to the appeal of local people by offering sufficient cots and beds to look after the boys 'who were going to attend the school for a couple of weeks. Kitchen utensils were also provided so that if the pupils liked they were able to live in that hall.
I hold in .my hand a page from a small rural newspaper published in that district, and because it tells an interesting story I should like to read a short extract. The paper is dated January 5 of this year, and says:
A youth's training class for girls will be held about February 15. In order that rural girls may participate in these classes it will be necessary for them to remain in town for a period of two weeks. The club therefore makes a special appeal to the residents to provide lodging for these girls.
In exchange for these services residents may be asked to accept farm produce such as wood, meat, vegetables, butter, et cetera.
Then on the 30th of March, over two months later, indicating that the course must have lasted longer than two weeks, I find this: Youth Training Course Closes
The provincial youth training course was brought to a successful close on Friday afternoon when the club served a banquet to the class at the Elks', hall.
The instructors of the extension department of the Saskatchewan university expressed great

Unemployment-Youth Training
satisfaction in the class of sixty-five young women, the largest during their ten months' term.
On Saturday afternoon the work of the girls was on display at the Masonic hall and tea served to a number of visitors from town and district.
According to the dispatch sixty-five girls from the immediate district spent a certain length of time receiving instruction from teachers in the extension department and then went back to their own homes. Some of them will go into employment away from home; some will stay at home but will be better fitted to carry on their daily labours in the sphere in which they were before the school was held.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey), speaking in this house about a month ago. referred to the small percentage of those who were given employment following a course at such schools or receiving other training given by the administration. But I say. Mr. Speaker, that it does not matter very much whether those taking this training afterwards go away from home to get a job for money hire, or whether they simply return to their homes, better equipped for a lifetime of service, to lead a more satisfactory life all round and to be of more use to the community round their own homes. So I say that it does not always matter whether a pupil secures occupation outside his or her own home. The important thing is that opportunities to acquire that knowledge were given, were accepted, and that afterwards came the opportunity to use the knowledge so acquired.
In small towns in the district of which I speak classes were held for young men and girls. There were also classes for the training of boys in motor mechanics. In Saskatchewan, which has suffered so severely in recent years from natural causes, there have been for the past two years, at any rate, youth training schemes in force at the university of Saskatoon, and boys and girls from all over the province have been accorded scholarships and taken into the university to study courses lasting from three to five months in various subjects. I know that the short-term course in agriculture has been most useful to many young men from the rural parts. I visited in January the diesel training school in motor mechanics which was earned on part of the time at the technical school in Saskatoon, and for the rest of the course at the university, and I could see from the progress that was made by some of the young men attending that the training was well worth while. I have been in touch with quite a number of young men during the past few years, as at the present time, and I have received many
letters from young men over a wide area of country telling me what they were learning, the progress they were making, what they wanted to do, and telling me every once in a while of jobs they had secured as a result of training received, and of the pleasure they were getting out of the training and out of the work to which it led.
I want to deal for a moment with the training of youth in industry. My good friend the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Mac-Nicol) made a statement that I believe to be absolutely correct. He said, if I understood him aright, that there was a dearth in this country of trained mechanics, and I think he was right; and in the years to come there is going to be a greater dearth of trained mechanics, not only in aircraft but in many other lines, if something is not done by industry and the authorities to give young people an opportunity to learn these trades. But I do not know that I would agree with my hon. friend when he suggested, if I heard him correctly, that industry could not afford to train young men. My belief is that industry cannot afford not to train them, because if industry does not train them, with a little assistance perhaps from the authorities, and that would be all right, how is industry going to perpetuate itself? That is a serious problem and more attention should be given to it.
Some two years ago I met, in the province of Saskatchewan, a noted British shipowner, Captain Dalgleish, of Newcastle-on-Tyne, of whom I am sure many hon. members have heard, owner and managing director of the shipping company that pioneered the Hudson bay route and whose ships have been successful on that route. He told me that one of the great mistakes which the British people had made during the early years of the depression was to allow the apprentice system to go out of use. The result was that when they needed mechanics they were not available. He told me that two years ago last fall, before he left England, he had to go to the secretary of the labour union and tell him that his company needed more engineers and found none available for work in the shipyard in which he was interested. The government had previously asked him to close that yard because they wanted to rationalize industry and combine that particular yard with others, but he had refused to do it because he said the yard would be needed again. While he may be old in years, he is younger than many of us in energy and spirit. He refused to close his yard because he foresaw that it would be required, and the time came when he wanted more engineers.
He went to the secretary of the union, and he was told that the only place where he

Unemployment-Youth Training
could get engineers was from the ranks of the superannuated. So he went to the superannuated and, commencing with three old men from among their ranks, by the time he had left England for Canada he was employing fourteen from the ranks of the superannuated and they were doing good work in the yard. This is what he said, and I thought it was significant. At the beginning these men were a little slow in their work; they were not able to turn out as much as the younger men could; but at the end of three months they were able to do practically as much as they had ever done, and the value of what they did was as great as it had ever been, because, he said, skill had never left their fingers, and after they had "suppled up" a little in their work they were just as good as they had been before. Now, to get men whose fingers had retained their skill through the years, through the period of superannuation and perhaps of unemployment that preceded it, there had been great skill developed in those fingers in their working days. "But," said Mr. Dal-gleish, "we made a great mistake, because the apprenticeship system has not been maintained, and so we have not available the number of skilled men we should have and the number that was available at one time." I believe that if there should come the world struggle which so many people believe to be unavoidable, and which everyone of us hopes yet may be avoided, victory is likely to rest with the country which has the greatest number of well-trained and highly skilled mechanics and workers of all kinds.
A good deal has been said in the past few hours and few sessions regarding scholarships. I think they are very important. I am glad to see that the minister has made provision in the bill which is now before us for enough money to devote some of it, as we hope he will do, to scholarships. Canada has already done something along that line. The Canadian people have always placed a high value upon education, and I believe its value will be increasingly recognized in the days to come. But it is not a problem for governments only or for the official authorities of any part of the country, dominion, provincial or local. I believe that the providing of scholarships is something which should appeal to our wealthier citizens, to those who, like Andrew Carnegie, Donald Smith and other men who have been great benefactors of their fellow men on this continent and in the old land, had not obtained a high degree of academic knowledge in their young days, but who appreciated the loss they had sustained, and who, when they came into pos-

session of wealth, set aside much of it to encourage education. I believe we have many people in Canada to-day who would respond to a lead to provide sums of money for tire training of the less fortunate youth of our land.
The state has been providing scholarships in some degree. I noticed in the press a few days ago an item recording the winners of forty-one or forty-two scholarships given by the national research council. Seven of those scholarships went to the province in which I live, and the names of the seven recipients were published at that time. The amounts ranged from $650 to $750 or thereabouts, and were for further study and research. I think that is something which should be encouraged. This country has not been wholly negligent of its young people. I believe we have done more under the circumstances than almost any other country has done to help young people in some ways which will be useful. I, too, have seen the civilian conservation corps men in the United States in training and moving round their camps and coming and going. I agree that these camps have done useful work so far as they have gone, but I do not know whether they are fitting their young men to stand on their own feet more successfully after they come out of the camps. I do not know whether they are making the men more self-reliant. I am not sure that they are enabling them to fight their own battles better after they come out than before they went in, assuming they are the right type of boys. If you encourage people to lean on government for everything, to allow government to do their thinking for them, to feed them, clothe them, tell them when to get up and when to lie down, and all the rest which goes on with regimentation, it is questionable-or rather it is not questionable at all, it is certain-that it will be difficult for them to preserve their initiative if that course of training is carried on for any length of time. However, that is our neighbours' problem; it is not ours.
I hope that the forestry work which will be carried on under this measure will proceed more in the way that lumbermen or forestry men actually do their work than in the manner in which army or civilian conservation corps training camps are conducted in the country to the south of us. I believe this would be better for the state and for the boys who are getting their training. Above everything, I would deprecate the using of our youth under this or any other legislation in the way in which the totalitarian states of Europe are using them. The hon. member for Weybum (Mr. Douglas) was to-day quite laudatory of

Unemployment-Youth Training
Germany for the way in which she is training her youth. I think it is terrible, the worst thing which could befall the youth of any country, that they should be taken and used in the way in which they are being used for the purpose for which the totalitarian nations intend them when "the day" comes.
I said at the beginning of my remarks that many of our people were suffering from discouragement because of the infection which has spread from Europe to this country, because of ideas which are different from those of the pioneer forefathers in this country. It is not so much because the simple necessities of life are absent, at least in rural areas, that many of our young people are suffering. To give them, when they are confused, the encouragement which is forthcoming through a measure of this kind is of the greatest value to them. To give them the training they can acquire, the exact knowledge they can get in forestry and mining classes, geology or mineralogy, agriculture and industry, which may be provided under this bill, will be of the utmost assistance to them, will help them to get over difficult places on life's road, will give them time to think and to orientate themselves while they are acquiring that skill of their hands and judgment of their heads which will enable them to enjoy useful lives in this country and will enrich the state many times over for what is going to be spent on them.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OP YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: The bill of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), for which I wish every success, is a bill for the training of young people to fit them for gainful employment. With all due respect to the government and to the minister I fail to see where there is any gainful employment obtainable in Canada through this measure, with all the changes in tariffs, quotas, favoured nation treaties, lowering of tariffs, dislocation of industry, and ruin of our home market. The bill is on the wrong basis. The scheme deals with unemployed young people between sixteen and thirty years; it has had a year for trial, and now the minister wants it to have a longer term trial of three years, involving expenditure over that three year period of approximately $4,500,000. That all looks very rosy if you take it at its face value, but when you get down to brass tacks you find that the government of the day have spent one-third of the amount of money which they expended on relief-I think all told it is about $900,000,000, on relief, dominion, provincial and municipal-

speechtext: Since 1930.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROMOTE AND ASSIST TRAINING OP YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
-I say that one-third of
that, or $300,000,000 has been spent on roads, uneconomic roads, away in the back concessions of Quebec, Ontario and the Northwest Territories, and from coast to coast. It is all very well for the hon. member who preceded me to speak as he did; he comes from Saskatchewan, whose premiers for many years have believed in free trade for the grain industry. If the industrial provinces of Ontario and Quebec, to which this scheme very largely applies, were to have one iota of the protective measures which Saskatchewan is receiving, the industries of Ontario would not ask for a bill like this, No. 94, and would not need the aid it provides, but would train these apprentices themselves. They would not need it.
Ever since the start of this bill I have had very little faith in it. In the first place I do not believe in the system. I believe that after a year's trial the system has been weighed and found wanting. First as to the parties; the government of Canada deals directly with the provinces. Those who wish to come under it have to go through a circuitous routine; sums have to be appropriated for these young people, and there are the provisions of the Interpretation Act about who are unemployed young people; they have to register with the employment service and be certified by the clerk and the appropriate provincial authority and all that.
To get down to brass tacks, if the minister would follow the principle which has been opposed by hon. members opposite for many years, namely the system of bonuses, subventions and subsidies as applied under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in agriculture and in the fishing industry, and apply some of the millions that are being spent in Saskatchewan on agriculture, in bonuses and subventions and subsidies for the industries of this country that would operate a proper apprenticeship system, we would get somewhere. I was a member of a board of education and a school board; I have talked to many teachers not only in the public schools but in separate and high schools of the city from which I come, and many of them are very much disappointed with this scheme. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey), the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and I have, in our ridings, several of the largest secondary schools, high schools and technical schools and collegiates in the country; I have consulted with those who go to these institutions and with teachers and members of the school boards, and they are very much disappointed with this scheme.

Unemployment-Youth Training
In the first place who is in charge? Many industrialists are keenly interested in education ; they are on university boards, school boards and all kinds of boards of education; why are they not used to head this department of youth training? Why should the government go to the pulpit and get as the head of this department a former minister? I have nothing to say against him; he is a fine man but he is not a practical man, he has not had the necessary business and industrial training.
In connection with this subject last year I think I read from the discussion in the United States, where the Purvis commission got some of its recommendations regarding youth training and youth employment, showing that gainful employment is not to be had. There is not an industry in Canada to-day that is working full time fifty-two weeks in the year.
Let me read three or four lines of the Couzens report on unemployment and industry and youth to the United States senate. At page 495, section 2 it says:
To say that all industries are seasonal would hardly be an exaggeration. It would be most difficult to find an industry which showed an even distribution of production and employment throughout the year. An individual plant here and there, to be sure, may show steady and regular employment from month to month, but such plants are exceptions and by no means the rule in any industry.
The bill is based on wrong premises, because gainful employment will not be forthcoming. One of the saddest sights to be seen is the jobless. It is saddening and sickening to see these young transients, many of them from the high schools, riding the rods and sometimes losing their lives. I have here a dispatch dated Ottawa December 29, stating that a man was taken off the train at Arnprior frozen and had to be taken to the hospital. At Timmins Magistrate Atkinson said he had noticed a large number of such cases, when seven youths came before him charged with vagrancy, their only offence being that they could not find work. This is an indication of the growing seriousness of the unemployed youth problem. The magistrate in passing sentence in the Timmins police court said:
It is a terrible indictment of our social conditions that young men should be sentenced to gaol simply because they cannot find work.
The board of education of Toronto have a technical school system. That city is spending almost $13,000,000 in maintaining schools of all kinds and education; every year these children come out of the schools and are unable to find employment. I get every week fifteen or twenty letters on the subject. If

we had a proper national apprenticeship system with industry and national service with it such as they have in the old country, where industrialists take charge, it would give the youth a better system. As I said a year ago:
The urgent need of the present day is to control the entry of juveniles into employment, to make the termination of full time schooling coincide with that entry, to modify or eliminate all regulations or examinations which are obstacles rather than aids to that transition, and to ensure that the first years of employment shall be treated as years of training and continued education. This policy involves, first of all, not merely an educational but an industrial reform; the imposition on organized industries of a statutory duty to formulate their schemes or recruitment and training, or in other words a revival in a new form of the idea of apprenticeship as the path to a definite professional status. It involves in the second place an extension of compulsory full time school attendance, not to some fixed and unalterable point dictated by the requirements of school courses, but to points corresponding with the various approved recruitment schemes of industries.
Thirdly it means a new cooperation between the state and industry in the establishment of a system of part time education, designed to assist the gradual transition from full time school to full time employment and to combine a continuation of general education with the training of industrial skill. Finally it means the encouragement during full time school life of every contact with practical, including occupational, life outside the school which does not endanger health or unduly interfere with school work.
In our educational example one of the chief weaknesses of the body politic is the dislike manifested by many of the most enlightened industrialists, who are really keen on education, for any organized system of part time education and part time employment.
This idea needs careful testing before it is put into practice. As I say, many of these industrialists are keenly interested in education. There is the five day working week during which the employed juveniles receive training in the factory, with the universal system of Saturday morning continuation classes.
The industrialists of this country have not shown the interest in this work that they should. And I can tell hon. members why. It is because of the instability of business, of the tariff, of these foreign agreements and tariff tinkering, giving our home markets to others with the result that industry does not know where it is at, cannot expand, and fears to do anything. Therefore industrialists are lukewarm towards the minister's scheme or any scheme that would be proposed by this government after the fashion of the Purvis report. The chairman of that commission is the head of Canadian Industries Limited. That company has underwritten a large number of industries in this country, engaged

Unemployment-Youth Training
in agriculture, transportation and distribution. What is he doing in some of his own industries? He is utilizing machines in a way never before known in this country. He is a director of one of the largest companies that I referred to yesterday, one of these public utilities where they installed an invention that means loss of work to 4,630 employees and a reduction of $3,000,000 to $4,000,000 in the wage bill. So I say I have little faith in this scheme because, owing to the instability of business in Canada, the industrialists will not take part in it.
Another thing is that industrial life is continually changing. You may have certain conditions in an industry in January, and in April different conditions altogether, and business practically eliminated or changed in it by September. We have seasonal, casual and technological unemployment. If we bonused the industries of this country to a small percentage of the extent we are bemusing the farming industry, the way the Minister of Agriculture is acting as Santa Claus on the prairies; if the industries of this country and the industrial provinces could have some of this Santa Claus treatment, we might get somewhere with an apprenticeship system, and not only solve the youth problem but aid in this emergency industrial power and, with it, national service for the emergencies bound to come to Canada soon. But when we have nothing but artificial barriers, restraints and burdens placed upon industry, not only in Montreal but in Quebec, Halifax, Vancouver, Hamilton, Toronto and all the other industrial cities, that cannot be done, for these employers do not know what security they have. If we had a few of these Santa Claus hand-outs for Saskatchewan, given to the men engaged in industry, they would be glad to enter into some sort of scheme with the provinces or this government under which they would look after the high school youths on a proper apprenticeship system, and all those who do not get into high school.
I criticize this scheme on another ground. It lacks modern education in its outlook and in its effect. There is too much book-learning and too much red tape; there is too much of going round in a circle in order to qualify so as to come under this measure. In all our education in this country there is too much dependence per se on mere book learning; we seem to forget to teach the duties of citizenship, love of country, service and sacrifice for our fellow men. Duty and patriotism seem to be almost forgotten.
Another point is this: What has become of the policy of the government in regard to Bill No. 94? The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and the Minister of National Defence 71492-210
(Mr. Mackenzie) should have had by now some national policy related to defence adapted to our circumstances. We may have a rude awakening by to-morrow morning. A very important speech is to be made tomorrow by a dictator. What have they done about the unemployed youth and national service in England? What have they done about the apprenticeship system there? I have referred to the way in which British industrialists, under a proper system, have taken advantage of part-time apprenticeship and part-time education to help look after the youth of that nation. The right hon. Minister of Labour in England, Ernest Brown, understands the situation. He went to the old city of York, where he saw a large number of men standing about the market place, youths from sixteen to twenty-four, and he took advantage of that opportunity to address the unemployed at a luncheon given in his honour by the council of that city. What is the trouble with the Minister of Labour? Some of the provinces ignore this government. Take the legislature of Ontario, which just closed its sessions an hour or so ago. They refuse to have anything to do with this government; they refuse to qualify under any of these schemes. They want a system of unemployment insurance such as they have in England. The Couzens report of ten years ago referred to the necessity for a proper system of unemployment insurance, and that would do more for the unemployed than all the minister's schemes, palliatives, quack remedies and patent medicines.
At the present time Quebec and Ontario are willing to enter into an unemployment insurance scheme. The minister of labour of Ontario, Mr. Hipel, put through a bill under which, if this house will pass enabling legislation, Ontario will enter into such a scheme; and if they cannot get a joint arrangement they will start a scheme of their own under the Ontario act. They are ready to go ahead and do something without waiting for the report of the Rowell commission, which really is not the Rowell commission any more, because unfortunately that able gentleman who has done so much for this country is no longer a member of that commission. But what will be done with the report of that commission if, as and when it is made? It will be buried in the archives of this government; "earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust."
Next Monday is May day. If this is all the Toronto members can offer the unemployed of that city, I am afraid there will be a very large delegation of the unemployed go to Queens Park and many other places. What



Unemployment-Youth Training
about the transients? There is very little ahead for them to-day, and there will be more coming out of the high schools on June 30. I saw some of them on the Canadian National right of way near Torrance. I talked with some of them, and they told me they were going to ride the rods right through to Vancouver and look for work until they found it. Some of them come from the finest homes in this country. Their fathers are out of work and they do not want to loaf round home, so they have taken to the road. We had 286 of these young men who had been housed all winter in the coliseum, tramping the streets yesterday. They have closed the coliseum to these poor transients and they are without house or food. The Reverend John Frank, the able young rector of Holy Trinity Anglican church near Eaton's store last fall opened a hostel for others.
This afternoon the minister said he did almost a little begging with the Ontario government in order to get a few more meals for the transients after April 15 and got it extended to May 1. Look at the millions they are spending on the prairies and tne millions they are spending on wheat! Why not announce a policy for those on relief under which there will be a greater domestic consumption of grain? They talk of these people going on the farms. Why, most of these young fellows who have been raised in the cities are not qualified for work on farms. If the government want to do something to feed the poor people on relief in a country with such abundance of plenty, let them go to work and use more of our domestic grain products; let them nationalize a portion of the wheat crop in order that the people on relief may use far more of the grain that is stored here for home consumption. To-day these poor transients are walking the streets of Toronto, without homes. The province will do nothing for them, and certainly they are not the responsibility of the municipality, because the minister announced that the transients were to be looked after by the provinces. I should like to refer to the bill itself in this connection:
(iii) deserving transients certified as eligible by an appropriate provincial authority.
There you have it again; they must go to Queens Park and have some provincial authority approve them as eligible to come under this scheme. The other day I received a letter from a gentleman in Owen Sound criticizing the lack of attention to getting work for transients and youth. He is Mr. Ivor Wagner, general manager of the Dominion Transportation Company Limited of Owen

Sound, which operates a large service all along the upper lakes, Georgian bay, lake Huron, lake Erie and the ports of that vicinity. He is a returned soldier, and he states the case for these transients in three paragraphs:
A few nights ago a young fellow, he wasn't any more than nineteen knocked at our door, and asked for the price of a bed and breakfast. He was clean-cut, intelligent and sober, just one of the great army of transients which call at the house almost every day. The next morning on my way to the office, I passed group after group of boys and girls of all ages heading for the nearby public and high schools. Happy, boisterous, carefree youngsters, and I wondered just what the future held for them *when school-days were over. How many of those eager, lively kids would join the army of transients tramping the country from one end to the other, aimless, hopeless, and demoralized. Not a nice thought is it? . . but real nevertheless.
Then my thoughts travelled back two and half years ago when I joined my old comrades on a pilgrimage to France to witness the unveiling of the Vimy Ridge war memorial. At that time I spent a week in Germany to see how our erstwhile enemies were faring. I was greatly amused to see the variety of uniforms everyone seemed to be wearing; the young men marching with brightly shined shovels over their shoulders, the nine and ten year old boys stepping out smartly with little haversacks on their backs; the young girls in brown shirts with swastikas on their arms; the storm-troopers and the regular army men. My Canadian up-bringing whispered . . . "It's all wrong, its medieval . . . you cannot regiment people forever." That was two and a half years ago, and I still am 100 per cent sold that democracy is the best bet. but as I look back, I cannot help but recall that the youth of Germany were clean, clothed and fed, and most important of all were absolutely sold on Germany.
I wonder if that young fellow who called at our door for a bed and breakfast is sold on Canada, or if our school boys and girls will be sold on Canada when, in a few short years, they step out as men and women? If they are not, then believe you me, it will be too late to start a sales talk on the benefits of democracy. No, I haven't got the solution, but I'm thinking darned hard.
What did they do about such conditions in England? At .the luncheon in the old city of York the minister of labour and the secretary of state for war announced a policy of national service under which the youths would sign up under the apprenticeship system for five years. They would get board, lodging, pocket money, training in industry, some military training for national service and deferred pay, and at the end could qualify for jobs in the air force as mechanics and pilots, and in other key industries. A policy like that, on a volunteer basis, adapted to Canada's circumstances, near the large centres of population, I have advocated for the last three sessions, with part-time apprenticeship and part-time eduction and vocational training. In that way these young men would be

Unemployment-Youth Training
serving their country. We may have a rude awakening to-morrow. A million young men under rearmament have been conscripted by the Chamberlain cabinet, to fight the battles of this empire alone against the dictators. It is all very well to say it should not be done. Would it not be far better if this government were to adopt a scheme of national service in Canada adapted to our circumstances, for our youth than to let those 268 men, who were turned out of the home last night, without food or shelter, go, without any provision for them? They might be in training schools part of the time. On Saturday mornings and at other times they might be engaged on some useful scheme such as that which has been developed by Mr. Brown, Minister of Labour in England. In Canada it could be a volunteer system, adapted to our local conditions on a volunteer basis and close to the larger industrial cities and bonused by the government with industry, or as a national scheme.
What has been the result after two years of trial of the present system in England? Many of these youths have been trained for industry. They can take jobs as mechanics or pilots in the air force, or in other key industries in Great Britain. In a year or two they will be full journeymen. They are doing something in the old land to get something done along this line and be ready for any national domestic service. Instead of doing anything in Canada we did practically nothing towards getting a good share of rearmament orders from Great Britain. I said last year something should be done to establish reserves of food, but nothing has been done.
Under another clause of this bill there is too much dealing with the provinces and too little direct contact with the municipalities and with their school boards and school systems in technical schools, vocational schools and that sort of thing.
Then, under this bill the suburban worker seems to have been entirely forgotten. He is the man who lives near the city, but he is altogether forgotten by the government. Instead of spending large sums of money on uneconomical roads in back townships, would it not have been far better to have spent part of that money in the largest cities of the dominion where a great number of the unemployed are located, and, instead of this bill, give bonuses and subsidies to industry and let industry take over this bill? It would be better to help industry engage in that way and run this system instead of the Department of Labour.
I may say I am very much disappointed in the scheme, because in my opinion it has been weighed in the balance and has been

found wanting. It is not training anything like the numbers it should train. I do not know what is going to become of the youth, unless the government develops a better system along the fines I have suggested, by which there will be very little interference on the part of the government. The government should supply some national policy for the country.
At the beginning of the session I asked if the government would secure immediately a national register of man power, industrial power, economic power and food power, so that we may be prepared in a time of emergency. Security is better than optimism. However, the government has done nothing. This is the seventy-fourth day of the session and we have done very little.
While I sympathize with the minister, and do not wish him to think our criticism is in any way personal, I must say that this problem has not been solved. In the United States many schemes have been tried, and they have been a failure. There have been experiments all over the world. There is no doubt the minister has had a hard time, as did his predecessors. It is a tiresome and thankless burden he has, and he can please nobody. But I must say I believe the minister would be far better employed if he were to apply a bonus system in industry whereby industry could look after that which is their function, namely a system like this of apprenticeships. I say that because so many of these industrialists are keenly interested in education in the universities and high schools of the country, and could better handle this program.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to criticize the bill, because, although it may be inadequate in many respects, undoubtedly it is a beginning. The latter part of the explanatory note to the bill should commend itself to hon. members.
It notes that the bill makes it possible for the government to carry out the purpose of the bill over a period of years, instead of only for one year, as was the case when assistance was given through the Unemployment and Agricultural Assistance Act. In this way the present measure is a great improvement, because it will enable the department to plan in advance.
In the explanatory note it is also stated that the general object of the bill is to promote and assist in the training of unemployed young people to fit them for gainful employment in Canada, and to supply the necessary administration and funds to that end. That is indeed a worthy object; but the difficulty which confronts not only the men who will be

Unemployment-Youth Training
inadequately trained under this measure, but men and women who leave training institutions efficiently and adequately trained, is that at the present time they cannot find work in gainful occupations.
I was impressed with the remarks of the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) when he said that our aim should be to get the people to rely on themselves rather than expect governments to do everything for them. I think the hon. member for Melfort must realize in his more thoughtful moments that we have passed through the stage where individual effort, without having regard to social requirements and social needs, is of great importance.
When my people came to this country some hundred years ago my grandfather took his axe, went out to the woods and cleared a place where he built a log house; and then he began to clear the land. He lived a very hard life. His children and his grandchildren went without necessaries of life, because the necessaries were not there. But that has all changed. The land has been cleared; the log house has given place to the frame house; the oxcart has been replaced by the automobile and the aeroplane; and, as I said the other day, production has been socialized so that it requires the cooperation of almost everybody. No one can begin to-day to make his own living without regard to his social surroundings. The hon. member for Melfort can no more do it than can I or the unemployed.
If we examine in the light of present developments the apprenticeship system, of which so much has been said, we realize that it has gone, perhaps never to return. In a large measure the machine has replaced the skilled worker. A certain amount of skill is required, it is true, but it is not the skill of the tradesman. In earlier days a man went into a shoe factory to learn about the making of shoes. He learned to carry out every operation from selecting the leather to making the finished shoe. To-day a man, or a woman for that matter, goes in to a shoe factory to tend a machine. If he becomes skilled, he may always remain at that one machine until he leaves the plant because of old age. A man entering a shoe factory to-day under such conditions knows no more about making shoes than a man who has never been in a shoe factory at all. What is true of the shoe industry is true of almost every other industry that can be mentioned. The skill that comes from long years of apprenticeship is gone, and because of precision machinery the need for that skill is gone. We might as well forget about that part of the program.

We must begin not only to train people to do things, but to train people in social and cooperative effort so that they may learn to work together as they must work together to-day. There is no provision for this in the bill so far as I can see. When I left eastern Canada thirty-one years ago I went west on a harvest excursion to Manitoba along with thirty-five thousand other people from various parts of eastern Canada. To-day the west has all the help it needs, the days of the harvest excursions are gone. What has happened in the agricultural industry has happened to an even greater extent in other industries. I give these illustrations to show the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and others just what is happening. Until we realize these things we are not going to make even a start in dealing with this problem of unemployed youth, unemployed adults and unemployed aged people.
My particular reason for rising to speak to-night is the statement which was made in the house yesterday by the minister in reply to a question by myself in connection with a certain number of unemployed young people in the city of Ottawa. I asked the minister if he had been informed that 110 men had been turned away the previous night from the Ottawa city mission, had had to spend the night in a building without beds, and were at that moment sitting on the sidewalk in front of the city hall. The minister's answer is reported on page 3232 of Hansard, where he said in part:
It has also been brought to the attention of the house that a considerable number of men have been placed in jobs through the employment office in Ottawa-100, in fact, in the week during which this group have been conducting demonstrations in the city of Ottawa.
Then, in answer to a further question by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), who wanted to know if the men had been advised where they might receive work or relief, the minister said:
I should hardly think it necessary to advise my hon. friend that there is one place where people can go if they are seeking work in the city of Ottawa-the employment service of Canada. In the week during which these men were conducting demonstrations in Ottawa, 100 men were placed through that employment service, some on farm work and some on the work being done by the Department of National Defence at Petawawa.

We want to know, what security is there; how much training is required; where it may be obtained; at what cost can the training be obtained; and is the proposed training adapted to equip one for any specific occupation?
